1) Suggest something slightly new: a walk somewhere fresh, a market, a class.
2) Keep it short enough to leave both wanting more.
3) Ask questions along the way.
4) End clearly: state whether you want a second date.
entries.myths: Thinking dinner-and-interview is the only date format. Doing something together builds more connection than another table.
entries.drill: Plan one slightly novel, short first date this week instead of dinner.

entries.title: Texting with respect
entries.science: There is no solid evidence for wait-two-days style rules. What works is warmth plus honesty: clear, kind messages that match the real relationship.
entries.studies: Huang et al. 2017: responsiveness, meaning listening, understanding, and caring, drove liking in conversations; timing rules like wait three days have no strong supporting study.
entries.practice:
1) Text like a normal person: when you want to and can.
2) Keep messages readable and kind.
3) Ask one real question instead of testing reactions.
4) If they are slow, assume life, not a game, until they show otherwise repeatedly.
entries.myths: Believing the double text is fatal. Repeated ignoring without explanation is the real warning sign, not the second message.
entries.drill: Send one honest, kind, no-game message to one person you like this week and observe the real result.

entries.title: Red flags to walk from
entries.science: Watch how a person handles no, small frustrations, and your boundaries. Fast over-the-top soulmate pressure, jealousy, guilt-tripping, and ignoring a clear no are signs to walk away.
entries.studies: Jonason et al. 2009: dark personality traits like narcissism and psychopathy predicted using short-term manipulation tactics in dating; love bombing itself is a popular label, not a clinical diagnosis.
entries.practice:
1) State one small boundary early and watch their reaction.
2) Treat guilt-tripping and mockery of your limits as serious data.
3) Do not accept soulmate-level intensity in week one.
4) Leave, tell a trusted person, and block if needed.
entries.myths: Thinking intensity equals love. Fast, pressuring intensity is a warning sign, not proof of devotion.
entries.drill: Write your three non-negotiable boundaries this week and share one with a trusted friend for accountability.

entries.title: Consent and respect
entries.science: Consent is a clear, enthusiastic yes for each step, and it can be withdrawn at any moment. Respect and honesty are the base of real attraction, not obstacles to it.
entries.studies: Jozkowski et al. 2014: college students read consent cues differently, which is why clear words beat guessing or assuming.
entries.practice:
1) Ask before escalating: physical contact, location changes, anything new.
2) No and not now are complete answers; do not negotiate them.
3) Check in during, not just before: 'Is this okay?'
4) Treat quiet as a stop, not a pause.
entries.myths: Thinking checking in kills the mood. Clear consent increases trust, safety, and closeness for both people.
entries.drill: Practice saying one clear consent check phrase out loud three times this week so it is ready when needed.

entries.title: Bids for connection
entries.science: A bid is a small move for attention: a comment, a sigh, a joke shown to you. Turning toward bids builds the friendship part of love.
entries.studies: Gottman & Levenson 1992: conflict dynamics predicted divorce across longitudinal studies; Gottman & DeClaire 2001 later built the bids-for-connection concept on this lab work.
entries.practice:
1) Notice one small bid from your partner today: a comment, a look, a sigh.
2) Turn toward it: look up, respond, engage for even ten seconds.
3) Track your turn-toward rate for a week.
4) Ask your partner what small bids they wish got more response.
entries.myths: Thinking only big gestures count. Daily small responses carry most of the closeness.
entries.drill: Answer ten small bids a day for a week and note how talks feel by day seven.

entries.title: Repair after conflict
entries.science: All couples fight. Stable couples repair faster: a joke, an apology, a hand, a timeout. Repair attempts are the skill, not avoiding conflict.
entries.studies: Gottman & Levenson 1992: how couples handled negativity during conflict predicted which marriages lasted; the popular 5-to-1 positive-to-negative ratio traces to this lab work, but independent replication is limited, so treat the exact ratio as Mixed.
entries.practice:
1) Agree on a stop signal before fights happen, like 'pause'.
2) Use it early, when voices first rise.
3) Cool down separately for 20 minutes, then return.
4) Whoever cools first names one thing they did wrong.
entries.myths: Thinking healthy couples never fight. They fight and then repair, again and again.
entries.drill: Agree on a pause signal this week and use it in the next disagreement, then return and repair within a day.

entries.title: The apology that lands
entries.science: A weak sorry fixes little. A real apology names the harm, owns your part, offers to fix it, and repeats different behavior next time.
entries.studies: Lewicki, Polin & Lount 2016: apologies with more parts worked better, and taking responsibility was the single most effective piece.
entries.practice:
1) Name exactly what you did: 'I snapped at you in front of our friends.'
2) Own it without but: 'That was on me.'
3) Offer a fix: 'Tonight I will clear the air with them.'
4) Change the behavior and check in later.
entries.myths: Checking a quick 'sorry?' from the other room. Apologies are actions, not just words.
entries.drill: Deliver one full four-part apology this week for a real small offense and follow the fix through.
entries.resource: The Five Languages of Apology (Chapman & Thomas)

entries.title: Attachment styles
entries.science: People tend to attach in patterns: secure, anxious (fears abandonment), avoidant (fears closeness), or a blend. Patterns are tendencies, not labels, and they can shift with safe relationships.
entries.studies: Hazan & Shaver 1987: adult romantic bonds follow attachment patterns first described in infants; later research shows these are dimensions, not fixed boxes.
entries.practice:
1) Read the four patterns.
2) Notice your pull: chasing, distancing, or steady.
3) In a hard moment, name the fear out loud to your partner.
4) Ask for what soothes it: 'I need a quick check-in, not a big talk.'
entries.myths: Thinking your style is your destiny. Patterns ease with awareness and safety; they are not verdicts.
entries.drill: Note your attachment pull in three tense moments this week and name the need underneath.

entries.title: Gratitude and responsiveness
entries.science: Feeling understood and appreciated is the core of closeness. Small thank-yous for everyday things do more than grand occasional gestures.
entries.studies: Algoe, Gable & Maisel 2010: expressed gratitude predicted greater connection in couples over time; Reis, Clark & Holmes 2004: perceived partner responsiveness organizes closeness and intimacy.
entries.practice:
1) Each night, thank your partner for one specific small thing.
2) Say what it meant, not just thanks.
3) Ask one question about their day and listen fully.
4) Do this for two weeks before judging.
entries.myths: Saving thanks for big occasions. Daily small appreciation is the steady supply.
entries.drill: Say one specific thank-you every day for a week and ask one real question about their day.

entries.title: Choose with eyes open
entries.science: Choose a partner on character, consistency, and how they treat people over time, not on checklist matching or early sparks. Watch how they handle no, money, stress, and friends.
entries.studies: Eastwick et al. 2014: meta-analysis found ideal-partner checklists barely predict real attraction and relationship success; lived experience is the better guide.
entries.practice:
1) List the five non-negotiable qualities you need, like kindness, honesty, and calm under stress.
2) Watch behavior, not promises, for three months.
3) Ask trusted friends what they see.
4) Walk away from broken non-negotiables, even if the spark is strong.
entries.myths: Believing love will fix character flaws. Patterns show up early and rarely bend to love.
entries.drill: Write your five non-negotiable qualities this week and have one honest friend check your dating pattern against them.
entries.resource: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (Gottman & Gottman)

description: Influence, negotiation, networking, and leadership — used fairly.

entries.title: Reciprocity
entries.science: People feel a strong pull to return favors, even small ones they never asked for. The pull is a fairness habit, not a debt contract, so it works even when the first gift was tiny.
entries.studies: Cialdini 2021: reciprocity is one of the core principles of influence; Regan 1971: students who got a free Coke bought more raffle tickets from the person who gave it.
entries.practice:
1) Give something real first: help, information, or a favor, with no strings.
2) Keep it small, useful, and personal, not expensive or showy.
3) Make your ask later, in clear words.
4) Never mention your gift while asking; let it stand on its own.
entries.myths: Myth: favors are a debt trap. You can accept a gift and still say no to a request. If a gift comes with obvious pressure, name it: 'Thanks, but I am not able to do that.'
entries.drill: Give one genuine, no-strings favor this week, like helping with a task or sharing a useful contact, and ask for nothing back.

entries.title: Commitment and consistency
entries.science: Once people take a small stand, they feel pressure to act in line with it. Small active commitments predict later, bigger actions.
entries.studies: Freedman & Fraser 1966: homeowners who agreed to a small safe-driving sign were far more likely to accept a large lawn sign later.
entries.practice:
1) Ask for a small, easy first step that fits what you both want.
2) Make the step active: written, spoken, or posted, not just a shrug.
3) Remind people of their own earlier words when a bigger ask comes.
4) Do the same for yourself: commit publicly to one goal.
entries.myths: Myth: pressure to stay consistent can never be questioned. If someone quotes your old words to corner you, you are allowed to update: 'I said that then, and my view has changed.'
entries.drill: Make one small public commitment to a goal this week, then take one action that matches it within two days.
entries.resource: Yes! 50 Scientifically Proven Ways to Be Persuasive (Goldstein, Martin & Cialdini)

entries.title: Social proof
entries.science: People copy what others do, especially when they are unsure. Seeing that most people do something quietly answers the question of what is correct.
entries.studies: Goldstein, Cialdini & Griskevicius 2008: hotel guests who read that most guests reuse towels reused their towels more than guests who read a standard green message.
entries.practice:
1) Show what most people actually do, not what they should do.
2) Use exact numbers from a real group: same hotel, same team, same street.
3) Pick a comparison group the person feels part of.
4) For people already doing well, add praise so they do not slide back.
entries.myths: Myth: any crowd number will do. Fake or vague numbers backfire when they feel manipulated. If a seller says everyone is buying with no proof, ask: do you have numbers, and from whom?
entries.drill: Find one true most-people fact about a group you belong to this week and use it honestly in one message.

entries.title: Authority
entries.science: People defer to experts and to signs of expertise, even when the sign is just a uniform or a title. Credible credentials cut through uncertainty fast.
entries.studies: Milgram 1963: ordinary people followed a lab-coat experimenter's orders to give what they believed were painful shocks, showing how far authority cues can push compliance.
entries.practice:
1) Show real credentials and experience before you advise.
2) Admit the limits of your knowledge out loud.
3) Point to where your claim comes from: data, training, or results.
4) For big decisions, say when a second expert should check.
entries.myths: Myth: titles are proof of truth. A title is a shortcut, not a guarantee. If an expert pushes you, ask for their evidence and for what the skeptics say.
entries.drill: Before advising anyone this week, state one honest limit of your expertise and one source for your main claim.

entries.title: Liking
entries.science: People say yes to people they like. Liking grows from genuine similarities, sincere praise, and cooperation toward shared goals.
entries.studies: Burger et al. 2004: people agreed to a request more often when the asker was said to share something small in common, like a first name or a birthday.
entries.practice:
1) Before you ask, find one real, shared interest and talk about it.
2) Give specific, deserved praise, not flattery.
3) Work together on one small thing first.
4) Keep your ask honest; do not charm past a clear no.
entries.myths: Myth: liking must be faked to work. Manufactured charm fails when it is spotted. If someone is too friendly too fast and then asks a favor, slow down and judge the request on facts.
entries.drill: Before one request this week, spend five minutes finding and naming one genuine thing you share with the person.
entries.resource: How to Win Friends and Influence People (Carnegie)

entries.title: Scarcity
entries.science: People want more of what is rare or running out. Limited supply and competition both raise desire, which is why deadlines and last-chance offers feel urgent.
entries.studies: Worchel, Lee & Adewole 1975: cookies in short supply were rated more valuable than identical cookies in plentiful supply, and most valuable when supplies had just dropped.
entries.practice:
1) Show true limits: real deadlines, real seats, real stock.
2) Explain why the limit exists.
3) Never invent or stretch a limit; fake scarcity destroys trust.
4) When the answer is no, accept it and leave the door open.
entries.myths: Myth: urgency equals importance. Fake countdowns are the classic manipulation. When a deal expires in one hour, ask what actually changes tomorrow before deciding.
entries.drill: In one useful offer this week, state the true reason for a real deadline, and let one no pass without pushing.

entries.title: Unity
entries.science: People favor those they see as one of us. Shared identity, like family, hometown, faith, or profession, changes who people will go out of their way for.
entries.studies: Cialdini 2016: unity was added as the seventh influence principle, distinct from liking; Tajfel 1970: even made-up groups made members favor their own side.
entries.practice:
1) Find the real group you share with the person: team, town, trade, or cause.
2) Name it early, before your ask, not during it.
3) Act in the group's interest first; identity is earned by contribution.
4) Keep the boundary honest; do not invent a we that does not exist.
entries.myths: Myth: shared identity is a free pass. Us talk is not consent. If someone wraps an ask in we are family or patriotism, separate the identity from the request and judge it plainly.
entries.drill: Do one concrete act for a group you belong to this week, like helping a teammate or answering a question in a community, before asking the group for anything.

entries.title: Combining the levers honestly
entries.science: The levers stack: a trusted expert who is liked, owes you a favor, and shows a real deadline is hard to refuse. Stacked as truth, this helps both sides; stacked as pressure, it triggers resistance.
entries.studies: Brehm 1966: people push back when they feel their freedom is being taken, a reaction called reactance, so heavy-handed pressure can produce the opposite of the intended result.
entries.practice:
1) Use a lever only when it is true: a real favor, a real limit, a real credential.
2) Pick one or two levers that fit the situation, not all of them at once.
3) Tell the person what is in it for them, in plain words.
4) Watch for pushback; if you sense an eye-roll, stop and switch to plain talk.
entries.myths: Myth: more techniques means more persuasion. A pile of tactics reads as manipulation. The test: would you be comfortable if the other person saw your private reasoning notes? If someone stacks tactics on you, slow the talk down and judge each claim on its own.
entries.drill: Plan one upcoming request this week using at most two levers. Write down why each one is true, and drop any that fail the honesty test.
entries.resource: Yes! 50 Scientifically Proven Ways to Be Persuasive (Goldstein, Martin & Cialdini)

entries.title: Resisting the levers
entries.science: Every lever can be used on you, often by people with something to sell. Knowing the names of the tactics lowers their power, and two calm questions cut through most of them.
entries.studies: Wood & Quinn 2003: across 17 studies, people who were warned about a persuasion attempt resisted it more, with a moderate average effect.
entries.practice:
1) When you feel a sudden urge to comply, pause for ten seconds.
2) Ask: what is being given, shown, or rushed here, and by whom?
3) Ask: would I say yes to this request without the gift, the crowd, or the deadline?
4) Buy yourself time with one sentence: 'Let me check and get back to you.'
entries.myths: Myth: resisting is rude. Saying let me think is normal and fair. Watch for the classic setups aimed at you: gifts before asks, everyone-is-doing-it claims, uniforms, flattery, and fake deadlines.
entries.drill: Keep a one-week log: each time you notice a lever aimed at you, in ads, shops, or email, write the lever's name and one line on how you responded.

entries.title: Framing: gain versus loss
entries.science: The same facts feel different depending on the frame. People avoid losses more strongly than they chase equal gains, so you will lose X moves people more than you will gain X.
entries.studies: Tversky & Kahneman 1981: in the Asian disease problem, people chose riskier options when the same facts were framed as losses, showing that frames change decisions.
entries.practice:
1) Decide honestly which frame fits: is this preventing a loss or improving a gain?
2) State the outcome first, then the proof.
3) Use loss framing for urgent risks, gain framing for opportunities and hope.
4) Never swap frames to manipulate; pick the frame that best reflects the truth.
entries.myths: Myth: framing is spin. Framing is choosing which true angle to lead with. If someone else flips the same numbers between gain and loss, ask for the raw facts before you decide.
entries.drill: Take one true message you must deliver this week and write it twice, once framed as a loss and once as a gain, then pick the more honest and fitting one.

entries.title: Social-norms messaging
entries.science: Telling people what most others actually do changes behavior in groups. It works best when the group is local, and it pairs well with approval for the good behavior.
entries.studies: Schultz et al. 2007: households using less energy than their neighbors increased use after a plain you-use-less note; adding a smiley of approval stopped the backslide.
entries.practice:
1) Say what most people truly do in this exact group, like most guests in this hotel.
2) Add approval for the behavior you want, saying it is valued here.
3) For people already doing well, skip the bare comparison and go straight to praise.
4) Never invent the norm or pick the version most flattering to you.
entries.myths: Myth: shaming works. Shame tends to push people toward the bad norm. Also beware the boomerang: telling people the wrong thing is common can make it more common, so pair the message with approval.
entries.drill: Write one social-norm message for a group you lead this week, with a true number and true approval, and use it once.

entries.title: Story beats statistics
entries.science: A story pulls people into the scene, and that feeling of being there is what changes minds. One concrete case usually sticks better than a page of averages.
entries.studies: Green & Brock 2000: readers who were more absorbed in a story, a state called transportation, shifted their beliefs more toward it, even when told it was fiction.
entries.practice:
1) Open with one real person, one moment, and what changed.
2) Keep the hero the audience, not you.
3) Use numbers only to confirm the story, not to replace it.
4) Keep stories true; one invented detail can sink the whole message.
entries.myths: Myth: a good story is automatically honest. Compelling stories can hide weak proof. If a pitch is all story, ask for the data behind it before you act.
entries.drill: Turn one dry fact you need to share this week into a 60-second true story about one person, and tell it once.

entries.title: Specificity
entries.science: Specific, concrete asks are easier to understand and easier to act on. Vague requests leave people unsure what to do, so they do nothing.
entries.studies: Borgida & Nisbett 1977: students chose a course more often after hearing one vivid, concrete account than after seeing the summary of many surveys.
entries.practice:
1) Name the exact action, time, and amount: not 'help us' but 'give two hours on Saturday'.
2) Give the reason in one clear line.
3) Show one concrete example of the action done right.
4) Remove every vague word: soon, some, whatever works.
entries.myths: Myth: smart people prefer abstract versions. Everyone acts more on pictures than on fog. If a request stays vague after you ask twice, treat that as a soft no for now.
entries.drill: Rewrite your next request this week with exact action, time, and amount, and send it to one person.

entries.title: Timing: when people are ready
entries.science: Persuasion lands when the moment fits. A message that arrives at the wrong time or after the decision is made just bounces off.
entries.studies: Gollwitzer 1999: people who formed if-then plans, naming the when and where of an action, followed through far more often than people who only intended to act.
entries.practice:
1) Before pitching, check readiness: is this decision even live right now?
2) If it is not live, plant the seed and stop talking.
3) When the moment comes, be brief and concrete.
4) Revisit quietly after a fair interval; good ideas age well.
entries.myths: Myth: the best pitch wins. A perfect pitch at the wrong moment loses to a weak pitch at the right one. Do not read someone's bad timing reply as a verdict on your idea.
entries.drill: Pick one person you have been meaning to persuade; this week, instead of pitching, ask one calm question that reveals their timing and readiness.

entries.title: Asking and following up
entries.science: People underestimate how often others say yes to reasonable requests. Asking directly helps more than hinting, and one polite follow-up is normal, not pushy.
entries.studies: Flynn & Bohns 2008: across field and lab settings, people underestimated by up to 50 percent the chance others would agree to their direct requests for help.
entries.practice:
1) Ask one clear person for one clear thing, in person or by direct message.
2) Say why them: 'you know this area'.
3) If there is no reply, wait three to five days and follow up once, adding a small new detail.
4) If the answer is no, or silence comes twice, thank them and stop; ask again only if something changes.
entries.myths: Myth: following up is annoying, so silence means no. One reminder is welcome and often needed; a third becomes pressure. Track what you asked and when.
entries.drill: Send one direct request you have been avoiding this week, then follow up once after five days if there is no reply.

entries.title: Interests versus positions
entries.science: A position is what someone demands; an interest is why they want it. Behind different positions there are often shared and compatible interests, which is where deals are made.
entries.studies: Thompson & Hastie 1990: negotiators in lab studies wrongly assumed interests were opposite even when trades were possible, and settled for worse outcomes than they could have reached.
entries.practice:
1) Before talks, write your position and beneath it the interest: what it gets you.
2) Guess the other side's interests, then ask open questions to check.
3) Look for where you care about different things: timing, certainty, scope, credit.
4) Offer a trade on the differences, not a split of the middle.
entries.myths: Myth: negotiation is a fixed pie. Many talks hide trades that cost you little and pay the other side a lot. Ask before assuming every win for them is a loss for you.
entries.drill: In one real negotiation this week, ask two questions about the other side's interests before naming any number.

entries.title: BATNA: your best alternative
entries.science: Your power in a negotiation comes from what you will do if the deal fails. A strong alternative, and the other side sensing you have one, changes the whole conversation.
entries.studies: White & Neale 1991: reservation prices and alternatives to agreement set the boundary of what negotiators accept, and better alternatives predict better final outcomes.
entries.practice:
1) Write what you will actually do if there is no deal, in concrete steps.
2) Improve it before the talk: a second offer, a smaller scope, a waiting option.
3) Set your walk-away number from that plan, not from feelings.
4) Let your confidence show quietly; you do not need to announce your alternative.
entries.myths: Myth: you should never reveal your alternative. Naming a real alternative can be a strong, honest signal; inventing one you do not have is a fast way to lose the room.
entries.drill: Before your next negotiation this week, write your real best alternative and one concrete way you will strengthen it before the talk.

entries.title: Anchoring and first offers
entries.science: The first number in a negotiation pulls the whole discussion toward it. First offers predict final prices, and whoever sets the anchor usually gains.
entries.studies: Galinsky & Mussweiler 2001: in three experiments, whichever side made the first offer reached a better outcome, and first offers strongly predicted the final settlement price.
entries.practice:
1) Research a defensible range before the talk.
2) If you are prepared, make the first offer: ambitious but justifiable.
3) Justify the number with real reasons so it holds up.
4) If they anchor first and low, refocus on your target and your alternative, not theirs.
entries.myths: Myth: a low first offer always wins. A weak anchor gets dismissed or insults the other side. The counter to someone else's anchor is your own prepared reasons, not outrage.
entries.drill: For your next negotiation this week, prepare one page: your target, your range, and three reasons that justify your number.

entries.title: Calibrated questions
entries.science: Calibrated how and what questions hand the problem back to the other side and invite them to solve it. They avoid yes-or-no answers and keep you talking without giving ground.
entries.studies: Voss 2016: the FBI negotiator credits calibrated questions, like 'how am I supposed to do that?', for moving hard cases; this is a practitioner method with limited controlled research, so treat it as promising, not proven.
entries.practice:
1) When asked for something impossible, do not say no; ask how we can make that work.
2) Collect their answers without judging them out loud.
3) Follow up with: what does a fair version look like to you?
4) Keep your own numbers and deadline out of the early answers.
entries.myths: Myth: a clever question beats honesty. If you use questions to dodge and stall forever, people notice. Use them to understand and solve, not to trap.
entries.drill: In one real conversation this week, replace one no or that-will-not-work with one honest how question.

entries.title: Silence as a tool
entries.science: Staying quiet after an offer or a question gives the other side room to talk. People often volunteer information or soften terms to fill the pause.
entries.studies: Voss 2016: pausing after an offer is a core practitioner move in hostage and business negotiation; formal lab evidence is thin, so use it as a light, low-risk habit.
entries.practice:
1) After you ask a question or state a number, count five slow breaths before adding anything.
2) When they pause, do not rescue the moment; let them think.
3) Write your instant reactions down instead of saying them while you wait.
4) Break the silence first only when the discomfort is yours, not the deal's.
entries.myths: Myth: silence creates awkward failure. Most people talk into silence and reveal their position. Do not use silence as a weapon in personal talks; use it as patience, not punishment.
entries.drill: In one conversation this week, after asking a question, let ten seconds pass before you speak again.

entries.title: Win-win vocabulary
entries.science: Calling a deal win-win is not what makes it one. Joint gains come from finding real differences and trading across them, and the label alone changes nothing.
entries.studies: Thompson & Hastie 1990: fixed-pie thinking pushed negotiators toward worse deals even when win-win options were available, showing the label is no substitute for the search.
entries.practice:
1) Drop the phrase win-win from your first draft; describe the actual trade instead.
2) List two things you value differently from the other side.
3) Propose the exchange in plain numbers or duties.
4) Check both outcomes at the end; if only one side gained, keep working.
entries.myths: Myth: a win-win label equals a fair deal. The words are marketing until the terms prove it. If someone repeats win-win but cannot describe your gain in concrete terms, ask them to.
entries.drill: Rewrite one proposal this week as concrete trades, you get X and I get Y, with no win-win label, and send it.

entries.title: When to walk away
entries.science: A negotiation is only worth doing if the deal beats your next best option. Walking away cleanly, with a good reason, often improves later offers.
entries.studies: White & Neale 1991: a BATNA, a reservation price, and a resistance point are three distinct limits, and negotiators often misjudge their own, as in their example of a buyer who budgets 200 dollars and leaves having spent 250.
entries.practice:
1) Before talks, decide the exact point where the deal stops being worth it.
2) Prepare a polite, no-blame exit line: 'This does not work for me, so I will pass.'
3) Walk slowly: state the reason once, without arguing, and keep the relationship.
4) Reopen later only if something real has changed.
entries.myths: Myth: walking away ends everything. A clean, reasoned exit often brings people back with better terms. Never threaten to walk as a bluff; it costs your credibility in every future talk.
entries.drill: Write your walk-away point and exit sentence for your nearest negotiation this week, and practice saying them out loud twice.

entries.title: Weak ties
entries.science: The people who help you most with news and jobs are often not close friends but friendly acquaintances. Weak ties move in circles you do not, so they bring information you cannot get at home.
entries.studies: Granovetter 1973: contacts gave 56 percent of the jobs he studied; of those who found jobs through contacts, most used people they saw occasionally (55.6 percent) or rarely (27.8 percent), with only 16.7 percent using someone they saw often; Rajkumar et al. 2022, testing 20 million LinkedIn users, found moderately weak ties produced the most job moves.
entries.practice:
1) List ten friendly acquaintances from past jobs, courses, or teams.
2) Expect most help to come from the lightest, most distant ones.
3) Keep light contact: a comment, a congratulations, a short note.
4) Ask distant ties for information and perspective first, and favors rarely.
entries.myths: Myth: only close friends matter. Close friends often know the same openings you do. Also, weak does not mean worthless: the tie still needs to be real and a little warm.
entries.drill: Reach out to two friendly acquaintances this week with a genuine message about something they are doing, and ask for no favor.

entries.title: Givers versus takers
entries.science: People with a giving habit who also protect their time end up with the best reputations and networks. Givers who never say no burn out at the bottom; takers get found out.
entries.studies: Grant 2013: across studies of engineers, medical students, and salespeople, givers appeared at both the bottom and the top of success, and the top givers gave in ways that also served their own goals.
entries.practice:
1) Give small, useful things often: a tip, an introduction, a thoughtful answer.
2) Give in ways that cost you little but help a lot.
3) Set limits: 'I can do ten minutes, not the whole project.'
4) Keep a short list of what your close contacts need and check it monthly.
entries.myths: Myth: giving means saying yes always. Pure selflessness invites free riders and burnout. If someone only asks and never gives back, say no sometimes and watch what happens.
entries.drill: Do one small, cheap, helpful thing for two different contacts this week, and decline one request that would cost you too much.

entries.title: Introvert-friendly networking
entries.science: Networking does not require being loud. Depth beats breadth for quieter people: one real conversation, prepared questions, and good listening build better contacts than working a whole room.
entries.studies: Grant, Gino & Hofmann 2011: introverted leaders got better results than extraverted ones when their teams were proactive, because they listened to ideas instead of taking over.
entries.practice:
1) Go to events with a goal of two real conversations, not meeting everyone.
2) Prepare three open questions before you arrive.
3) Arrive early, when crowds are small and talk is easy.
4) Leave when your energy drops; thirty focused minutes beat three strained hours.
entries.myths: Myth: introverts cannot network well. The loudest networker is not the best connected. If a big scene drains you, change the format: coffee, walks, and one-to-one talks count fully.
entries.drill: Have two one-to-one conversations this week, by coffee or call, with prepared questions, and skip any large event.

entries.title: The follow-up asset
entries.science: Most contacts fade from silence, not from dislike. A light, specific follow-up keeps the door open, and old connections reactivate well, often better than strangers do.
entries.studies: Levin, Walter & Murnighan 2011: executives who reconnected dormant ties for work advice got useful, fresh knowledge efficiently, and old strong ties kept their trust even after years apart.
entries.practice:
1) After any good meeting, send a short note within a day about one detail you liked.
2) Set a reminder to check in with key contacts every few months.
3) Use real reasons for contact: an article, a milestone, a quick question.
4) Reconnect with one dormant tie every week for a month.
entries.myths: Myth: they will remember me, so I can wait. Memory fades faster than you think. Two short contacts a year keep more doors open than any clever message.
entries.drill: Reconnect with one person you have not spoken to in over a year, by giving a real reason and asking one light question.

entries.title: Becoming the connector
entries.science: The person who introduces others gains a rare position: they hear about opportunities from every side. Brokers, people who link separate groups, get more novel information and better ideas.
entries.studies: Burt 2004: managers whose networks spanned separate groups, so-called structural holes, produced and were judged to have more valuable new ideas than those who stayed in one cluster.
entries.practice:
1) Spot two people, each in a different circle, who would genuinely help each other.
2) Make the introduction short and double opt-in: ask each side first.
3) Expect nothing in return, and say so.
4) Do this monthly and keep notes on who needs what.
entries.myths: Myth: connecting means collecting contacts. A connector adds value by linking, not by stockpiling names. If you make careless introductions, people learn to ignore your email.
entries.drill: Make one double opt-in introduction this week between two people who share a real interest or need.

entries.title: LinkedIn and alumni strategy
entries.science: Platforms like LinkedIn make weak and dormant ties easy to keep. The tool shows the network you already built, and light activity keeps you visible without awkward effort.
entries.studies: Rajkumar et al. 2022: in LinkedIn's randomized experiments, new moderately weak connections increased job mobility, showing that light platform ties do real work.
entries.practice:
1) Clean up your profile once: real photo, plain summary of what you do.
2) Send a connection note after meeting anyone, with one line about where you met.
3) Post or comment small, useful things weekly to stay warm.
4) Check your alumni network monthly and message one graduate in a field you like.
entries.myths: Myth: adding contacts equals a network. Numbers without warmth are noise. If you send mass, copy-paste requests, expect silence or the wrong kind of attention.
entries.drill: Send two personalized connection notes this week, one to a recent acquaintance and one to an alumnus in your field, each with a real sentence about why.

entries.title: What trust is made of
entries.science: Trust is built from three parts: ability, benevolence, and integrity. People trust you when you can do the work, seem to care about them, and follow honest rules.
entries.studies: Mayer, Davis & Schoorman 1995: their widely used trust model shows that perceived ability, benevolence, and integrity predict how much people will trust and rely on a colleague.
entries.practice:
1) Show ability: do one small task well and share the result.
2) Show benevolence: ask about their side and act on what you hear.
3) Show integrity: keep small promises, especially unglamorous ones.
4) When one part is weak, name it: 'I am new here, but I will be straight with you.'
entries.myths: Myth: trust is one feeling, all or nothing. Trust has parts, and each can be repaired separately. If ability failed, like a late delivery, fix reliability; a warm apology alone will not do it.
entries.drill: Pick one colleague this week and strengthen one weak part of trust: do a small task very well, ask about their concerns, or keep a tiny promise exactly.

entries.title: Why reputation compounds
entries.science: Reputation is built in repeated games, with the same people watching the same choices. Small fair acts today make the next deal easier, because people remember patterns, not cases.
entries.studies: Axelrod 1984: in computer tournaments of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, the simple strategy of cooperating first and matching behavior afterward kept winning, showing how fair patterns reward themselves.
entries.practice:
1) Treat recurring contacts as a repeated game: short-term tricks will be found out.
2) Cooperate first, honestly, with new people.
3) Respond firmly but fairly to bad behavior, then forgive when they change.
4) Track your pattern: what do people say about you when you are not there?
entries.myths: Myth: one clever win is worth a small lie. In repeated settings, liars get detected and the cost lands later with interest. If someone wins once at your expense, note it and adjust how you deal with them.
entries.drill: Do one small fair act this week that a recurring contact will notice, and write down what happens next.

entries.title: Apology and repair
entries.science: A good apology has parts: say what you did, accept responsibility, express regret, and state the repair. Apologies rarely erase damage, but they start the path back.
entries.studies: Lewicki, Polin & Lount 2016: apologies with more components, especially accepting responsibility and offering repair, were judged more effective; integrity violations were harder to repair than ability failures.
entries.practice:
1) Name the specific act; do not hint or generalize.
2) Say I was wrong, without a but.
3) State regret plainly and skip excuses.
4) Offer concrete repair, then change the behavior; a second apology for the same act counts for much less.
entries.myths: Myth: sorry you feel that way is an apology. It shifts blame back to the other person. Do not apologize just to get a fast answer; repair takes time and proof of change.
entries.drill: Write and deliver one real apology this week with all four parts, then take one concrete repair action within three days.

entries.title: Myth: Charm Can Outrun Delivery
entries.science: Charisma buys you attention, not trust. Trust grows from predictable behavior, when your small actions match your words over and over.
entries.studies: Cialdini 2021: the commitment and consistency evidence shows people judge you by your pattern of actions, so a charming performance with no follow-through buys only the first impression.
entries.practice:
1) Choose three small promises you will keep every week, like replying within a day.
2) Announce fewer promises; keep the ones you announce even when no one is watching.
3) When you will miss something, say it early and give a new date.
4) Let the pattern speak; skip speeches about your values.
entries.myths: Belief under test: charm covers inconsistency. Charming flakes are exciting once and costly twice. If someone's stories dazzle but their promises keep slipping, believe the pattern over the performance.
entries.drill: Pick one small weekly promise this week, like replying by end of day, and keep it every day for seven days without announcing it.

entries.title: Own your mistakes early
entries.science: Teams that treat mistakes as information learn faster. Owning an error early, with a fix, lowers its cost and often raises people's view of you.
entries.studies: Edmondson 1999: hospital teams that felt psychologically safe reported more errors and performed better, because errors were discussed and fixed instead of hidden.
entries.practice:
1) When you notice your error, say it before anyone asks.
2) State the impact plainly: who is affected and how.
3) Bring a fix or a choice of fixes.
4) Remember the price of hiding grows by the week; late errors cost more.
entries.myths: Myth: admitting mistakes damages your standing. Hidden mistakes damage it far more when they surface, and they always surface. Owning your error is not the same as announcing every self-doubt.
entries.drill: Within one day of noticing any error this week, send one short message: what happened, the impact, and your fix.

entries.title: Engineer your track record
entries.science: A track record is built from visible small wins that pile up. Looking reliable and productive over time comes mostly from steady, visible progress, not one huge moment.
entries.studies: Amabile & Kramer 2011: across nearly 12,000 daily diary entries, small daily progress was the strongest driver of positive work mood and motivation, feeding the record people build.
entries.practice:
1) Keep a simple log of shipped work: date, result, number.
2) Aim for one visible piece of progress each week, even a small one.
3) Share short updates with people who care, without bragging.
4) Every month, turn your log into one clear story for a review or an interview.
entries.myths: Myth: my work speaks for itself. Quiet work gets forgotten; evidence and retelling are part of the work. Keeping evidence is not boasting; it is bookkeeping.
entries.drill: Start a one-page results log this week with three past wins, then add one entry every day.

entries.title: Psychological safety
entries.science: Teams do their best work when members feel safe to speak, ask, and admit mistakes. Safety does not mean softness; it means candor without punishment.
entries.studies: Edmondson 1999: safe teams reported and discussed errors more and performed better; Google's Project Aristotle 2015, studying 180 teams, found psychological safety the top factor in team effectiveness.
entries.practice:
1) Model fallibility: say I may be wrong and thank people for pointing out problems.
2) Ask real questions and wait for answers.
3) React to bad news with curiosity first, not blame.
4) Protect the person who raises the hardest issue.
entries.myths: Myth: safety means lowering standards. It is the opposite: high standards plus honesty. If people are quiet in meetings and chaotic in private chats, safety is missing.
entries.drill: Ask your team or family one honest question about what could go wrong, stay silent for ten seconds, and thank whoever speaks first.

entries.title: Giving feedback (Situation-Behavior-Impact)
entries.science: Feedback lands when it names the moment, the behavior, and the impact. Judging character instead of describing actions triggers defenses and usually fails.
entries.studies: Kluger & DeNisi 1996: across 131 studies with 607 effect sizes, about a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, mostly by threatening self-image instead of describing behavior.
entries.practice:
1) Situation: name the time and place, like in this morning's meeting.
2) Behavior: describe what you saw, without labels, like you cut in twice.
3) Impact: say the effect on you or the work, like we lost Sam's point.
4) Ask what they saw, then agree on one next step.
entries.myths: Myth: honest feedback must feel harsh. Facts stated plainly are easier to hear than judgments. Sandwiching a real issue inside praise usually hides the message; state it directly and kindly.
entries.drill: Give one piece of feedback this week in the exact three steps, situation, behavior, impact, and ask one listening question afterward.

entries.title: Delegation
entries.science: Delegating work with real authority grows skills and frees your time. People do better when they own the problem and the choices, not just the steps.
entries.studies: Hackman & Oldham 1976: jobs with autonomy and whole tasks raised internal motivation and performance; delegation is how leaders create those conditions day to day.
entries.practice:
1) Hand over the outcome and the decision rights, not just the steps.
2) State the goal, the deadline, and the guardrails in one breath.
3) Agree on check-in points instead of hovering.
4) When they decide differently from you but it works, say nothing about the difference.
entries.myths: Myth: it is faster to do it myself. True for today, false for the year. If you keep taking work back at the first wobble, you teach people to wait for rescue.
entries.drill: Delegate one task this week with goal, deadline, and one checkpoint written down, and do not touch it in between.

entries.title: Running meetings people do not hate
entries.science: Most meeting misery comes from structure: no agenda, no time limit, no clear ending. Short, well-run meetings get more done and get judged fair even by busy people.
entries.studies: Rogelberg 2019: his surveys and studies of meetings show that meeting load and poor meetings relate to lower engagement, and that simple structure fixes most complaints.
entries.practice:
1) Have an agenda: each item with an owner and a time.
2) Default to 25 or 50 minutes, not a full hour.
3) End every item with a decision or a clear next step.
4) Cancel any meeting whose business could fit in a message.
entries.myths: Myth: more meetings mean more work gets done. Often the reverse: meetings crowd out the work they discuss. Ask once: if this meeting disappeared, what would break?
entries.drill: For your next meeting this week, cut the length by a third, send an agenda with owners, and end five minutes early with the actions read out.

entries.title: Credit-sharing
entries.science: Leaders who share credit build loyal teams and safer honesty. Taking credit for group work wins moments and loses people.
entries.studies: Grant 2013: reports the responsibility bias first shown by Ross & Sicoly 1979, where people claim more responsibility for joint work than their partners credit them; takers who act on this bias and take sole credit for team wins get punished, while givers who share credit keep their teams.
entries.practice:
1) Name contributors clearly in public: who did what.
2) Say we in wins, and I in mistakes.
3) Send a short note to a boss praising a teammate by name.
4) When praised alone for team work, redirect with one concrete name.
entries.myths: Myth: visible credit means less for me. Sharing credit rarely shrinks your standing and often raises it, because people see you lifting the group. Hiding others' work is what quietly sinks reputations.
entries.drill: Publicly credit one teammate this week by name for a specific contribution, and copy a person it would help.

entries.title: Leading without a title
entries.science: Influence on peers comes from what you give and how you make people feel, not from a job title. Enduring power is granted by the group, and it goes to the generous and useful.
entries.studies: Keltner 2016: reviewing decades of lab and field studies, he finds that influence is repeatedly given to those who are socially attuned and generous, and lost by those who turn harsh once powerful.
entries.practice:
1) Pick one problem nobody owns and quietly solve it.
2) Help a colleague look good in front of their boss.
3) Bring information and calm to tense moments.
4) Ask for nothing for a month and watch your influence grow anyway.
entries.myths: Myth: authority requires a title. Titles add leverage, not influence itself; many titled people have no pull. If your ideas keep dying in the room, your move is service and signal, not louder pushing.
entries.drill: Solve one small unnamed problem at work or home this week, tell no one you did it, and note who noticed.

entries.title: Dominance versus prestige
entries.science: There are two routes to standing: dominance, which works through fear and intimidation, and prestige, which is respect earned by skill and sharing knowledge. Prestige is slower but sturdier and far better liked.
entries.studies: Cheng, Tracy, Foulsham, Kingstone & Henrich 2012: in groups of strangers, both dominant and prestige-seeking people gained influence, but only the prestigious were liked; Cheng, Tracy & Henrich 2010: prestige went with advice-giving and prosocial traits, dominance with aggression and narcissism.
entries.practice:
1) In every new group, learn to spot the two types fast.
2) Invest in the prestige route: build a skill and share the know-how.
3) Use firmness when needed, but keep it tied to the task, not to intimidating people.
4) Do not copy dominant tactics you see; they end in resentment.
entries.myths: Myth: fear is the fastest route. Dominance does move people and draws attention, but it breeds dislike and quiet resistance. If a boss rules by fear, comply with what is fair, keep records, and do not rely on their favor.
entries.drill: Teach one useful thing you know to one person this week, in fifteen minutes, expecting nothing back.

entries.title: Status in every room (read before you act)
entries.science: Every new group forms a pecking order within hours, before anyone wins or loses anything real. Reading who holds attention, and who yields it, tells you how the room runs.
entries.studies: Cheng et al. 2012: in fresh groups, observers could already identify influential members quickly, and eye-tracking showed people's gaze going to both dominant and prestigious members.
entries.practice:
1) On entering a group, watch for ten minutes before talking much.
2) Notice who defers to whom, and who speaks last before decisions.
3) Address the room, not just the loudest person.
4) Be warm to every rank; the quietest person often holds one of the keys.
entries.myths: Myth: the loudest person is in charge. Volume can mark anxiety as often as power. Also do not confuse your first read with truth; hierarchies shift once real work starts.
entries.drill: In one meeting or group this week, stay quiet for the first ten minutes, then write down who influenced whom and why.

entries.title: Earning prestige
entries.science: Prestige is earned with two things: a skill people value and a will to share it. It compounds quietly, because people copy and recommend skilled, generous people.
entries.studies: Cheng, Tracy & Henrich 2010: prestige was tied to advice-giving, achievement, and prosocial traits; Henrich & Gil-White 2001: humans evolved to copy and defer to the most skilled and knowledgeable group members.
entries.practice:
1) Pick one skill that matters in your field and get measurably better each month.
2) Make your knowledge public: notes, demos, short teaching.
3) Answer questions patiently, including beginners' questions.
4) Keep generosity steady; prestige decays when sharing stops.
entries.myths: Myth: hiding expertise keeps your edge. Hidden skill earns nothing; shared skill earns status and still leaves you ahead, because trust and teaching raise your own level. If envy appears, keep sharing and keep improving.
entries.drill: Write one short explainer this week, a page, a post, or a five-minute talk, about a skill you have, and share it with your group.
entries.resource: So Good They Can't Ignore You (Newport)

entries.title: Status anxiety (do not chase the room's approval)
entries.science: Chasing everyone's approval keeps you anxious, because approval is local and temporary. Self-esteem works like a gauge of belonging; when you anchor to your own circle and values, the gauge steadies.
entries.studies: Leary et al. 1995: self-esteem tracked how accepted people felt, acting like a social gauge rather than a verdict; Anderson et al. 2012: respect within your immediate circle, not global rank, best predicted well-being.
entries.practice:
1) Notice when you crave one specific person's nod; ask what you would do if it never came.
2) Build your base: two or three people whose respect you truly have.
3) Measure your days by your own promises kept.
4) When comparison stings, zoom out to your circle, your values, and your plans.
entries.myths: Myth: enough status will finally end the anxiety. Chasing universal approval is a treadmill; respect from your real circle is the steady ground. Being liked by strangers is not the same as being trusted by your people.
entries.drill: Act once this week by your own judgment in a situation where you would normally wait for approval, and write one line about how the fear felt before and after.

entries.title: Status is contextual
entries.science: Status is not one ladder but many. You can be a big name in one room and a beginner in the next, and the same person can be respected at work and ignored at the gym.
entries.studies: Anderson et al. 2012: status measured inside a person's own group, not global standing, tracked well-being, showing that rank lives in local rooms, not in one overall score.
entries.practice:
1) Map your rooms: work, family, sport, online, and note where you stand high and low.
2) Do not import status from one room to another; earn each one fresh.
3) Where you are low, act like a learner: ask, help, improve.
4) Where you are high, remember how little it travels; stay humble.
entries.myths: Myth: status follows you everywhere. Respect is room-specific and must be earned again in each new place. If someone leans on old titles in a new room, watch how quickly the room stops listening.
entries.drill: Pick one room this week where you are a beginner, ask one honest question, and thank the person who answers.

description: Human nature, manipulation defense, and the hard situations nobody warns you about.

entries.title: Emotion comes first, reasons come second
entries.science: Feelings arrive before explanations. People decide quickly and intuitively, then build reasons to fit the decision. Greene treats this as a master law, which fits the evidence, though he stretches it into claims about hidden drives that research cannot measure.
entries.studies: Haidt 2001: moral judgments start as fast intuitions and conscious reasoning usually follows to justify them, matching Greene's law; his drive-reading exercises go beyond what the data supports.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: when someone argues very hard, ask what feeling is really at stake.
2) Counter the rush: say, 'I want to answer well, so I am taking a day to think.'
3) Judge actions over speeches; keep a short note of what was promised and what was done.
4) For your own choices, decide after a night of sleep, not after a spike of anger or excitement.
entries.myths: Mistake: assuming people's stated reasons are their real reasons, or that a strong emotion means a strong argument. Feelings are information about a person, not proof of a claim.
entries.drill: For 7 days, before agreeing to any request that stirs a feeling, wait 24 hours and write one line about the emotion you felt.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Everyone carries a self-centered streak
entries.science: People protect their self-image and see themselves as a little above average. Greene calls this the law of narcissism; research supports ordinary self-enhancement bias, while the idea that everyone is deeply narcissistic overshoots the data.
entries.studies: John & Robins 1994: students rated their own performance higher than observers did, and the gap grew with narcissism scores, though modest self-enhancement was common rather than rare.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it in yourself first: ask where you want praise more than truth.
2) When someone cannot admit a small error, do not debate their worth; describe the fact: 'The report was late. Let us fix the deadline.'
3) When a person flatters you heavily, check their next request twice as carefully.
4) Keep one friend who will tell you the truth, and thank them for it.
entries.myths: Myth: calling out narcissism wins arguments. Labels trigger defense. Describe behavior and consequences instead of character.
entries.drill: This week, ask one honest person for one unflattering piece of feedback, and thank them without arguing.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: We play roles, and masks slip eventually
entries.science: People adjust their self-presentation to fit the audience, which is normal social skill, not constant fraud. Greene's role-playing law is partly supported, but he tends to read calculated deception into ordinary politeness.
entries.studies: Snyder 1974: high self-monitors changed their behavior to match social cues and were rated as more adaptable; self-monitoring is a stable measured trait, not proof that everyone is fake.
entries.practice:
1) Spot the mismatch: watch how the same person talks to a boss, a rival, and a waiter.
2) Counter with patience: give new people ordinary time, and judge consistent patterns over weeks.
3) In decisions, weight what people do when no audience is watching.
4) If a story changes, ask neutrally: 'Help me understand what changed since last week.' Then compare the answers.
entries.myths: Mistake: believing you can read people instantly. First impressions capture performance skill, not character. Slow patterns are the real signal.
entries.drill: This week, observe one person in two settings, like a meeting and a casual lunch, and write one line about what stayed the same.
entries.resource: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (Goffman)

entries.title: Groups bend individual judgment
entries.science: People often go along with a confident majority even when the majority is clearly wrong. Greene's conformity law is well supported; the classic experiments still replicate, though the effect is smaller in some cultures and settings.
entries.studies: Asch 1956: many participants gave obviously wrong line-length answers to match a unanimous group; Bond & Smith 1996 meta-analysis of 133 studies: conformity is a reliable effect, though its size varies widely by culture, era, and task.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: a room going quiet, then agreeing fast, is a signal to slow down.
2) Counter alone first: write your own answer before hearing the group.
3) Say it plainly: 'Can we poll everyone privately? I want independent views.'
4) Make it safe for the first dissenter; invite the quietest person to speak first.
entries.myths: Myth: only weak people conform. Conformity rises with uncertainty and with status, so it hits experts too. Design the process so agreement is not required.
entries.drill: In one meeting this week, ask everyone to write their view before any discussion starts, then compare notes.

entries.title: Envy has two forms, one drives up, one drags down
entries.science: Envy is the pain of another person's advantage. Benign envy motivates self-improvement; malicious envy wants to pull the other person down. This part of Greene's law is well supported.
entries.studies: Smith & Kim 2007 review: envy is common and turns hostile when the advantage feels undeserved; van de Ven et al. 2009: benign envy raises effort while malicious envy raises pulling-down motives.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: sudden coolness or faint mockery after your good news.
2) Counter quietly: share wins with the likely envied gently, without gloating.
3) When you feel envy, name it, then convert it into one concrete step of your own progress.
4) If the digs continue, say once: 'That sounded like a jab. Did you mean it that way?' Then share less with that person.
entries.myths: Myth: envy is always hidden hatred. Much envy is friendly and motivating. Also do not label every critic envious; sometimes the criticism is right.
entries.drill: This week, write down one person you envy and one skill of theirs, then practice that skill for 20 minutes on two days.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Frustration feeds aggression, especially when goals are blocked
entries.science: Blocked goals raise the odds of aggression, though frustration alone rarely causes violence. Greene treats frustration as a direct cause; the modern view says it is one trigger among many, filtered by self-control and provocation.
entries.studies: Berkowitz 1989: the frustration-aggression link was reformulated as an anger readiness rather than an automatic reflex; Catalano, Novaco & McConnell 2002: layoffs were linked to more violence among laid-off workers while feared layoffs linked to less; Catalano et al. 2011 review: job insecurity and economic decline are linked to worse mental health and well-being.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: people lash out when tired, crowded, or blocked from a goal.
2) Counter with space: 'This is not the moment. Let us pick this up at 4 pm.'
3) Lower the stakes in the moment: offer a smaller, real choice.
4) In yourself, treat hunger, fatigue, and looming deadlines as aggression warnings.
entries.myths: Mistake: venting anger by shouting gets it out of your system. Catharsis often increases hostility. Cooling off works better than blowing off.
entries.drill: For 7 days, when you feel irritation rising, pause for ten slow breaths and note the blocked goal behind it.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Grandiosity inflates claims and invites a fall
entries.science: People high in grandiosity feel special, entitled, and exempt from rules, and they overestimate their results. Greene's grandiosity law is supported for narcissistic traits; his sweeping claim that everyone is grandiose most of the time is not.
entries.studies: Leckelt et al. 2015: narcissists are seen as charming early but lose popularity as conflicts and derogation build; grandiosity predicts admiration at first, then conflict over time.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: 'I alone' stories, rule-skipping, and irritation at small corrections.
2) Counter with records: 'Let us check the numbers together.'
3) Hand the person one visible win early, then hold every later claim to evidence.
4) Watch your own stories: remove one 'I did it all' sentence this week.
entries.myths: Mistake: believing confidence means competence. Measured confidence and tested delivery are different things; ask what the person actually built.
entries.drill: This week, rewrite one success story you tell about yourself with the word 'we' where it belongs.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Moods and loyalties shift faster than you expect
entries.science: People mispredict how long feelings will last and how much events will matter. Greene's fickleness law captures something real about shifting moods and attention; he again overreads it as calculated betrayal.
entries.studies: Wilson & Gilbert 2005: affective forecasting errors are common, and people overestimate the intensity and duration of future feelings, so today's enthusiasm says little about next month's.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: today's champion of an idea was lukewarm last week.
2) Counter with repetition: say, 'Let us write down what we agreed, so neither of us has to rely on memory.'
3) Re-test commitments at a normal moment, not during excitement.
4) Keep plans flexible enough to survive a change of audience.
entries.myths: Mistake: taking every change of mood personally. Much fickleness is ordinary mood drift. The pattern to track is promises breaking repeatedly.
entries.drill: This week, after any enthusiastic yes, confirm the plan in one calm sentence 48 hours later and note what changed.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Suppression is real; classic repression is shaky
entries.science: Greene's law of repression says painful feelings and memories get pushed out of mind. Thought suppression and motivated forgetting are real, but the Freudian claim that trauma memories are routinely repressed and then recovered is not well supported.
entries.studies: Wegner et al. 1987: trying not to think of a white bear made the thought return more, the rebound effect; Anderson & Hanslmayr 2014: people can weaken unwanted memories through control processes, which is motivated forgetting, not full repression.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: 'I am fine' followed by avoidance, unexplained slips, or overreactions.
2) Counter gently: 'You do not have to tell me anything. I am around if it ever helps to talk.'
3) Do not push for a dramatic recovered memory; support steady, ordinary coping instead.
4) For your own hard feelings, name them to yourself daily for a week.
entries.myths: Myth: if you cannot recall it, it must be repressed. Memory gaps have many causes, and suggestion can create false memories. Handle memory claims with care and evidence.
entries.drill: For 5 days, write two lines each evening naming one avoided feeling and one small action you took anyway.
entries.resource: The Laws of Human Nature (Greene) - read critically

entries.title: Awareness of death shapes how people defend their world
entries.science: Reminders of death make people cling harder to their own group, values, and heroes. Terror management is well studied; Greene integrates it fairly, though the effects are moderate and depend on context.
entries.studies: Rosenblatt et al. 1989: mortality reminders made judges set higher bail for a disliked defendant, the classic effect; Burke, Martens & Faucher 2010 meta-analysis: the effect is reliable and moderate in size across many studies.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: existential moments, like funerals or crises, harden group lines.
2) Counter with perspective: at tense times, say, 'Let us agree on the practical goal first, and leave the larger argument for a calmer day.'
3) Do not debate worldviews during a scare; revisit the practical question when emotions settle.
4) In yourself, use mortality gently: let it prioritize what matters, not frighten you into others' hands.
entries.myths: Mistake: assuming fear of death explains most behavior. The effect appears in specific primed conditions; it is one influence among many, not a master key.
entries.drill: This week, write one page on what you want your life to stand for, then schedule one hour for the thing you listed first.
entries.resource: The Worm at the Core (Solomon, Greenberg & Pyszczynski)

entries.title: The dark triad: three related, overlapping traits
entries.science: Machiavellianism, narcissism, and subclinical psychopathy overlap in callous manipulation but differ in flavor: strategic, entitled, or cold. These are personality dimensions measured in normal ranges, not diagnoses, and most people with higher scores are not dangerous.
entries.studies: Paulhus & Williams 2002: the three traits are distinct yet correlated, sharing a callous-manipulative core; O'Boyle et al. 2012 meta-analysis of 245 samples and 43,907 people: all three linked to counterproductive work behavior, and the authors say the triad explains a moderate amount of the variance in it.
entries.practice:
1) Spot the shared core: charming, low empathy, rule-bending, and tests of your boundaries.
2) Counter with evidence: judge patterns of behavior over months, not personality guesses.
3) Never tell someone they are a dark-triad type; say instead, 'I want to talk about what happened, not who you are.'
4) Run the reverse check on yourself before judging: is there a normal explanation?
entries.myths: Myth: dark triad means psychopath or evil. Scores are subclinical traits; mental health diagnoses require professionals and much more than a quiz.
entries.drill: This week, read one real description of the dark triad measures, such as the Short Dark Triad, and note two ways the pop version exaggerates it.

entries.title: Psychopathy in everyday life
entries.science: Subclinical psychopathy mixes low empathy, impulsivity, and boldness. Most claims of a psychopath epidemic in offices are overstated; meta-analytic leadership evidence shows only weak links, and severe cases are rare in general populations.
entries.studies: Landay, Harms & Crede 2019, 92 samples: psychopathy weakly predicted emerging as a leader, weakly predicted lower effectiveness, and moderately predicted less transformational leadership; the authors conclude popular fear of psychopathic leaders is overblown.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: shallow emotion after harm, blame-shifting, thrill-seeking at others' cost, no repair behavior.
2) Counter with distance: keep shared work written and specific, and do not expect insight or empathy to appear.
3) Decide with the pattern, not the apology; say, 'I am looking at what changed, not what you promise.'
4) In dating, watch how they treat someone who cannot help their career.
entries.myths: Myth: about 1 in 25 people is a psychopath. That pop figure is misquoted; estimates for the full clinical pattern are around 1 percent, and it appears far more in prison settings than in offices.
entries.drill: This week, list three behaviors you would treat as final deal-breakers, and hold one boundary without over-explaining.

entries.title: Narcissism: charm up front, costs later
entries.science: Narcissism predicts being noticed and rising into leadership, but not being good at leading. The pattern is reliable: early appeal, later conflict, especially when the person feels criticized.
entries.studies: Grijalva et al. 2015 meta-analysis: narcissism predicted leadership emergence but had no linear link to effectiveness, with a midrange optimum (inverted U); Back et al. 2010: at zero acquaintance, narcissists were judged more attractive and likable, and Leckelt et al. 2015: that popularity advantage erodes over months as rivalry and derogation grow.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: quick charisma, name-dropping, little curiosity about you.
2) Counter with time: watch how they handle a small error, a shared win, or a polite no.
3) Separate charisma from competence: ask what they built without applause.
4) If pressure starts, use one line: 'I like the idea. I still decide on evidence and time.'
entries.myths: Mistake: equating narcissism with confidence. Healthy confidence does not collapse when criticized, and it does not require constant admiration.
entries.drill: This week, after any impressive first meeting, write one line about how the person treated someone with less power.

entries.title: Machiavellianism: strategy, not superiority
entries.science: Machiavellianism means treating people as tools for goals. The evidence does not show a master manipulator who wins long term: results are mixed, and short-term gains often come with reputational and performance costs later.
entries.studies: O'Boyle et al. 2012: higher Machiavellianism predicted somewhat lower job performance and more counterproductive behavior; Qin & Xu 2013: the overall link with job performance was near zero, with small negative links to income and job satisfaction; Marbut, Harms & Crede 2025, 163 samples: Machiavellian leaders were on average neither rewarded nor penalized while showing links to poor follower outcomes.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: flattery with an angle, information hoarding, loyalty tests.
2) Counter with clarity: put agreements in writing and copy the right people.
3) Share less strategically sensitive information with people who collect leverage.
4) When an ask feels angled, say: 'Send that in writing with the scope and the credit split, and I will answer tomorrow.'
entries.myths: Myth: manipulation always wins in business. Evidence shows mixed results and rising costs; over the long run, reputation loss cancels the gains.
entries.drill: This week, before one cooperative project, write the split of credit and work openly with your partner.
entries.resource: The Prince (Machiavelli) - context, not a playbook

entries.title: Spotting dark patterns in dating
entries.science: Some dark-triad traits correlate with exploitative dating behavior and infidelity, but the links are small. Charming, fast-moving people are usually not dangerous; the risk pattern is pressure plus punishment when you hold a boundary.
entries.studies: Strutzenberg et al. 2017: in one cross-sectional sample of 484 college students, excessive early attention correlated with narcissistic tendencies; Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar 2025 meta-analysis of 11 articles: dark traits showed small positive correlations with infidelity, about .13 for narcissism, .23 for Machiavellianism, and .25 for psychopathy.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: declarations of love in days, pressure to commit fast, irritation when you keep one evening for yourself.
2) Counter with pace: 'I like you. I move slowly with everyone, and that is not changing.'
3) Keep your friends in the loop; isolation is the main warning sign.
4) Do not test people with games; watch how they handle your normal needs.
entries.myths: Mistake: assuming any slow or inconsistent partner is a manipulator. Inconsistency is common and human; the warning is a pattern of pressure and punishment, not mixed signals alone.
entries.drill: This week, tell one friend the single behavior you would treat as a stop sign in dating, and write it where you will see it.

entries.title: Spotting dark patterns at work
entries.science: Dark traits are somewhat more visible at work through rule-bending, credit-taking, and charm that fades after promotion. Evidence on leaders with moderate dark traits is mixed, so the safe test is behavior and reputation, not scores.
entries.studies: Kückelhaus, Meurs & Blickle 2024: high-Machiavellian employees developed worse reputations and lower performance ratings when low in political skill, while higher political skill buffered that harm rather than creating an advantage, showing context matters more than the label.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: fast rise, thin delivery record, blame spreading downward.
2) Counter with documentation: after meetings send one-line summaries of who owns what.
3) Build your own reputation for clean delivery; it protects you when credit is disputed.
4) If pushed to cover for someone, say: 'I will report what I did and what I saw. I will not sign off on the rest.'
entries.myths: Mistake: thinking you can screen people with an internet quiz. Dark-triad scales are research tools, not hiring or marriage tests, and they do not predict individual cases well.
entries.drill: This week, start a simple work log of what you delivered and when, no complaints, just facts.

entries.title: Gaslighting: making you doubt your memory
entries.science: Gaslighting is a repeated denial of events that makes a person doubt their own memory and judgment. The term began as a play and a clinical idea; empirical research is developing, mostly from domestic violence studies, so treat the findings as emerging.
entries.studies: Warshaw et al. 2014 (survey reported in Sweet 2019): in a survey of 2,500 callers to a domestic violence hotline, 73.8 percent said a partner deliberately did things to make them feel crazy; this describes a high-risk help-seeking group, not the general population. Graves & Samp 2021: among 298 adults, gaslighting reports were higher at both low and high levels of relationship power than at moderate levels.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: 'You are remembering it wrong' repeated only with this person, until you keep saying 'maybe I am too sensitive.'
2) Counter: 'That does not match what I remember. I am checking my notes.'
3) Keep notes with dates in a place only you control.
4) Verify one story with an outsider before doubting yourself again.
entries.myths: Myth: if someone denies your memory once, they are gaslighting you. People honestly misremember. The pattern is repeated denial plus pressure to accept their version over yours.
entries.drill: For 7 days, keep a short dated log of key conversations and feelings, and re-read it once before any conflict.

entries.title: Love bombing: affection as a hook
entries.science: Love bombing is a rush of intense attention, gifts, and promises very early, creating fast attachment and a debt of feeling. It becomes manipulative when it is paired with isolating you, demanding total devotion, or punishing ordinary limits.
entries.studies: Strutzenberg et al. 2017, an early empirical study on love bombing: excessive early communication correlated with narcissistic tendencies and lower self-esteem in one cross-sectional college sample of 484; the research base is young, so read this as emerging evidence, not settled law.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: 'You are my soulmate' within days, huge gifts, and irritation when you step out of the script.
2) Counter by pace: 'I like you too. I still move at a normal speed. Let us keep this to weekends for now.'
3) Return expensive gifts with a warm explanation.
4) Keep your own schedule, friends, and sleep; a true partner survives the word 'later.'
entries.myths: Myth: intensity equals love. Intensity equals speed, and one intense person may simply be intense. The pattern is intensity plus control and punishment for slowness.
entries.drill: This week, hold one evening for your own interests and watch, without drama, how the people closest to you respond.

entries.title: Guilt trip: making you pay for normal choices
entries.science: Guilt is a social emotion that can be used to move people to comply. The healthy version points to a real repair; the manipulative version trades on a vague debt that you can never repay.
entries.studies: Baumeister, Stillwell & Heatherton 1994 review: guilt is a common and often prosocial interpersonal force, and it can be exploited to extract compliance beyond any real debt.
entries.practice:
1) Spot it: 'After everything I have done for you' applied to a routine request.
