2) See an orthodontist if you have bite or jaw concerns.
3) Focus on sleep, strength, and grooming.
4) Ignore before-and-after posts that use angles and lighting.
entries.myths: Believing mewing grows a sharp jawline in adults.
entries.drill: Skip mewing for a week and spend the time on sleep or one strength session instead.

entries.title: Jaw trainers: weak evidence, real risks
entries.science: Chewing devices may work the jaw muscles, but they do not change bone or remove fat. Overuse can cause jaw pain and temporomandibular joint problems.
entries.studies: Verma et al. 2024 reported two users with no visible jaw change after about three months and found limited evidence for jaw exercisers. Dental reviews warn that heavy chewing can aggravate jaw joints.
entries.practice:
1) Do not buy a device that promises a new jawline.
2) Stop if you feel jaw pain or clicking.
3) See a dentist for jaw pain.
4) Use proven levers: body fat, grooming, and posture.
entries.myths: Believing a rubber chewing device will give you a model jawline.
entries.drill: Skip jaw trainers for a week and note whether your jaw pain or clicking changes.

entries.title: Height tricks: what actually works
entries.science: Shoes, insoles, and posture can add a little apparent height. Exercise cannot make bones grow after the growth plates close.
entries.studies: Proffit et al. 2018 describe growth plate fusion in the late teens to early twenties, after which long bones stop growing. No exercise or stretching changes bone length at that point.
entries.practice:
1) Wear shoes that fit and add a modest lift if you like.
2) Stand tall and avoid slouching.
3) Choose well-fitted clothes that lengthen the leg line.
4) Do not lie about your height.
entries.myths: Believing stretching, hanging, or special exercises make adults taller.
entries.drill: Check your posture and shoe fit this week; skip height-growth exercises.

entries.title: Face yoga: emerging at best
entries.science: A small pilot study found modest changes in cheek fullness after 20 weeks of facial exercise. The study was uncontrolled and small, so treat face yoga as experimental.
entries.studies: Alam et al. 2018 studied 27 middle-aged women; 16 completed 20 weeks of facial exercises and showed modest improvement in cheek fullness and estimated age. There was no control group and many dropouts.
entries.practice:
1) If you enjoy it, keep it short and gentle.
2) Do not expect a new face.
3) Do not replace sunscreen or sleep with it.
4) Stop if it causes jaw or facial tension.
entries.myths: Believing face yoga reverses aging or replaces proven skin care.
entries.drill: Try five minutes a day for a week and judge honestly; stop if it causes tension.

entries.title: Dysmorphia warning: stop looksmaxxing into misery
entries.science: Body dysmorphic disorder affects about two percent of adults and is much more common in cosmetic settings. If appearance distress is driving repeated procedures, get screened before going further.
entries.studies: Veale et al. 2016 estimated BDD prevalence at 1.9 percent in the community, 13.2 percent in cosmetic surgery, and 20.1 percent in rhinoplasty settings. The review shows that appearance distress is common and often under-recognized.
entries.practice:
1) Set a daily limit on looks checking and photos.
2) Pause before booking another procedure.
3) Talk to a doctor or therapist if distress affects your life.
4) Remember that BDD is treatable.
entries.myths: Believing one more procedure will finally make you feel good enough.
entries.drill: Track looks-checking time for three days; if it is over 30 minutes a day or causes distress, talk to a doctor or therapist.

entries.title: Why muscle matters
entries.science: Strength training supports health, mood, and daily function, not just appearance. It is one of the best investments you can make in how you feel and move.
entries.studies: Momma et al. 2022 found muscle-strengthening activities were linked to a 10 to 17 percent lower risk of death and major diseases. Gordon et al. 2018 found resistance training reduced depressive symptoms with a moderate effect.
entries.practice:
1) Start with two sessions a week.
2) Train the whole body.
3) Keep a simple log.
4) Increase slowly over time.
entries.myths: Thinking lifting is only about vanity or bulky muscles.
entries.drill: Schedule two strength sessions this week and do the first one even if it is short.
entries.resource: The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Training (Helms et al.)

entries.title: Progressive overload
entries.science: Muscles grow when training gets gradually harder. Add a rep, a little weight, or a set when you can, instead of doing the same workout forever.
entries.studies: The ACSM 2009 position stand describes progressive overload as a core principle of resistance training. Schoenfeld et al. 2017 found that more weekly sets were linked to more muscle growth, showing that dose matters.
entries.practice:
1) Log your exercises and reps.
2) When you hit the top of your rep range, add a little weight.
3) Keep form clean before adding load.
4) Do not change everything every week.
entries.myths: Thinking you must confuse muscles by changing exercises constantly.
entries.drill: Log four sessions this week and add one rep or a small amount of weight each time.

entries.title: Volume and frequency
entries.science: More weekly sets per muscle, up to about ten or more, tend to produce more growth. Training each muscle about twice a week is a reasonable starting point.
entries.studies: Schoenfeld et al. 2017 found a graded dose-response, with 10 or more weekly sets per muscle linked to more growth, though that category was a trend. Schoenfeld et al. 2016 found two sessions per week may be slightly better than one for hypertrophy.
entries.practice:
1) Count weekly sets for each muscle.
2) Aim for about 10 sets per muscle per week.
3) Split them over two or three days.
4) Add volume slowly and recover.
entries.myths: Thinking more is always better and training every muscle daily.
entries.drill: Count sets for one muscle this week and adjust toward 10 per week.
entries.resource: The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Training (Helms et al.)

entries.title: Beginner program shape
entries.science: A simple full-body program two or three times a week builds strength and muscle. Compound movements and consistency matter more than a complicated split.
entries.studies: ACSM 2009 recommends two or three sessions per week for novices, with compound exercises and gradual progression. Schoenfeld et al. 2016 supports training each muscle about twice a week.
entries.practice:
1) Choose a squat, hinge, push, pull, and carry.
2) Do two or three sets of five to twelve reps.
3) Rest between sets.
4) Add a little weight or a rep each week.
entries.myths: Thinking you need a six-day bodybuilding split to start.
entries.drill: Do two full-body sessions this week with five simple exercises each.

entries.title: Protein: about 1.6 grams per kilo
entries.science: Total daily protein around 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight supports muscle gains. More than that gives no extra benefit for most people.
entries.studies: Morton et al. 2018 meta-analyzed 49 trials and found protein supplementation helped, with a breakpoint at about 1.62 grams per kilogram per day. Above that, gains in fat-free mass did not increase further.
entries.practice:
1) Include protein at each meal.
2) Spread it across the day.
3) Use food first; shakes are optional.
4) Ask a doctor if you have kidney disease.
entries.myths: Thinking you need three grams per kilogram or a shake within seconds of training.
entries.drill: Estimate your protein for three days and add one protein-rich meal or snack.
entries.resource: The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Nutrition (Helms et al.)

entries.title: Creatine: evidence and safety basics
entries.science: Creatine monohydrate is one of the best-studied supplements for strength and muscle. It is safe for healthy people and may add a little water weight.
entries.studies: Kreider et al. 2017, the International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand, found creatine monohydrate is effective and safe for healthy people. A common maintenance amount is three to five grams a day; ask a doctor if you have kidney problems.
entries.practice:
1) Choose plain creatine monohydrate.
2) Take it daily, with or without food.
3) Drink water normally.
4) Do not expect it to replace training.
entries.myths: Believing creatine is a steroid or damages healthy kidneys.
entries.drill: If interested, buy plain creatine monohydrate and take it daily for a week with water.

entries.title: Consistency beats optimization
entries.science: Showing up regularly with basic training explains more progress than a perfect program. Missing one session is not failure; quitting is the real risk.
entries.studies: Morton et al. 2018 found training itself accounted for far more variance in gains than protein supplements. ACSM 2009 emphasizes regular, progressive training over complex routines.
entries.practice:
1) Pick a schedule you can keep.
2) Put sessions in your calendar.
3) If you miss one, do the next one.
4) Deload or rest when you are run down.
entries.myths: Thinking you must find the perfect program before you start.
entries.drill: Book three sessions in your calendar next week and do the first one even if it is short.
entries.resource: The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Training (Helms et al.)

entries.title: Seven to nine hours: the consensus
entries.science: Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep. Regular short sleep is linked to worse health, mood, and thinking.
entries.studies: Hirshkowitz et al. 2015, the National Sleep Foundation consensus, recommends seven to nine hours for adults. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society reached a similar conclusion.
entries.practice:
1) Set a bedtime that allows eight hours in bed.
2) Keep wake time consistent.
3) Protect sleep from late work and screens.
4) Stop treating sleep as optional.
entries.myths: Thinking you can train yourself to need five hours with no cost.
entries.drill: Choose one bedtime and keep it for seven nights.

entries.title: Poor sleep shows on your face
entries.science: Sleep-deprived people look more tired, less healthy, and less attractive. Observers can pick up sleep loss from faces alone.
entries.studies: Axelsson et al. 2010 found observers rated sleep-deprived faces as less healthy, more tired, and less attractive. Sundelin et al. 2013 found sleep deprivation increased visible cues such as hanging eyelids, red eyes, dark circles, and pale skin.
entries.practice:
1) Prioritize sleep before buying more skin care.
2) Keep a consistent schedule.
3) Make the room dark and cool.
4) Compare a photo after a normal night with one after a short night.
entries.myths: Thinking concealer or a filter fixes the effects of chronic sleep loss.
entries.drill: Take a photo after a normal night and one after a short night this week and compare.

entries.title: Sleep hygiene that matters
entries.science: Light, caffeine timing, temperature, and a consistent schedule affect sleep more than most gadgets. Keep the room dark and cool and give yourself a wind-down.
entries.studies: Drake et al. 2013 found that caffeine taken even six hours before bed disrupted sleep in a controlled study.
entries.practice:
1) Dim lights and screens an hour before bed.
2) Keep caffeine earlier in the day.
3) Cool the room.
4) Get up at the same time every day.
entries.myths: Thinking alcohol is a good sleep aid.
entries.drill: Pick one sleep hygiene change and do it for seven nights.

entries.title: Naps: short and early
entries.science: A short early-afternoon nap can improve alertness. Long or late naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night.
entries.studies: Brooks & Lack 2006 compared naps of different lengths and found a 10-minute nap improved alertness and performance, while a 30-minute nap caused temporary sleep inertia. Leong et al. 2022 found afternoon naps had small to medium cognitive benefits.
entries.practice:
1) Keep naps short, around 10 to 20 minutes.
2) Nap early in the afternoon.
3) Avoid napping late in the day.
4) Do not use naps to replace regular sleep.
entries.myths: Thinking a two-hour nap is always good for you.
entries.drill: Try one short early-afternoon nap this week and note your alertness afterward.

entries.title: When to see a doctor: snoring and apnea
entries.science: Loud snoring, gasping, and daytime sleepiness can be signs of sleep apnea. Untreated apnea is linked to serious health risks, so get it checked.
entries.studies: Young et al. 2008 followed the Wisconsin Sleep Cohort for 18 years and found severe untreated sleep-disordered breathing was linked to about 3.8 times the all-cause mortality risk. Treatment matters, so see a doctor if you have symptoms.
entries.practice:
1) Ask a bed partner whether you snore or gasp.
2) Note daytime sleepiness and morning headaches.
3) See a doctor if symptoms are present.
4) Do not rely on phone apps for diagnosis.
entries.myths: Thinking snoring is just annoying and never dangerous.
entries.drill: If you snore loudly or wake gasping, book a doctor visit this week.

entries.title: Mediterranean pattern
entries.section: Nutrition & Stress Basics for Looks & Mood
entries.science: A Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, olive oil, fish, and nuts is linked to better heart health and mood. The pattern matters more than one superfood.
entries.studies: Estruch et al. 2013, the PREDIMED trial, found a Mediterranean diet reduced major cardiovascular events. Lassale et al. 2019 found healthier diets were linked to lower risk of depression.
entries.practice:
1) Build meals around plants and beans.
2) Use olive oil instead of butter often.
3) Eat fish or other protein regularly.
4) Limit ultra-processed food.
entries.myths: Thinking one superfood or supplement fixes everything.
entries.drill: Eat one Mediterranean-style meal every day this week.

entries.title: Eating for skin and energy
entries.section: Nutrition & Stress Basics for Looks & Mood
entries.science: A balanced diet with enough protein, fruit, vegetables, and water supports overall health and energy. Claims that one diet transforms skin are usually overstated.
entries.studies: Lassale et al. 2019 found better diet quality was linked to lower depression risk. Estruch et al. 2013 found a Mediterranean pattern improved health outcomes. No diet has been proven to cure acne, so see a dermatologist for severe acne.
entries.practice:
1) Include protein at each meal.
2) Eat fruit or vegetables at most meals.
3) Drink water through the day.
4) Avoid cutting out whole food groups without a reason.
entries.myths: Thinking a detox, lemon water, or one elimination diet clears skin forever.
entries.drill: Add one vegetable and one protein to lunch every day this week.

entries.title: Caffeine and alcohol realities
entries.section: Nutrition & Stress Basics for Looks & Mood
entries.science: Caffeine boosts alertness but can harm sleep if taken late. Alcohol may make you sleepy at first, but it fragments sleep and can leave you looking tired.
entries.studies: Drake et al. 2013 found caffeine six hours before bed still disrupted sleep. Ebrahim et al. 2013 reviewed alcohol studies and found it reduces sleep onset but increases disruption in the second half of the night.
entries.practice:
1) Keep caffeine earlier in the day.
2) Switch to water between alcoholic drinks.
3) Avoid alcohol as a sleep aid.
4) Protect your sleep schedule.
entries.myths: Thinking alcohol improves sleep quality.
entries.drill: Move your last caffeine earlier and have two alcohol-free days this week.

entries.title: Stress shows on skin and sleep
entries.section: Nutrition & Stress Basics for Looks & Mood
entries.science: Stress can worsen skin conditions and sleep, which then makes both look worse. Slow breathing and basic stress habits help break the loop.
entries.studies: Chen & Lyga 2014 reviewed the brain-skin connection and found stress can increase inflammation and worsen skin conditions. Zaccaro et al. 2018 found slow breathing can shift the body toward a calmer state.
entries.practice:
1) Do five minutes of slow breathing.
2) Take a short walk outdoors.
3) Limit doomscrolling before bed.
4) See a doctor if stress or skin problems are severe.
entries.myths: Thinking stress is all in your head and cannot affect your skin or sleep.
entries.drill: Do five minutes of slow breathing every day this week and rate stress and sleep.

description: Intelligence, memory, learning, and thinking tools.

entries.title: The g factor, plainly
entries.science: People who do well on one mental test tend to do well on others, and that shared pattern is called general intelligence, or g. It is a statistical summary of how abilities cluster, not a single organ or a single skill. It helps predict who will learn complex material faster, but it says little about any one person's future.
entries.studies: Schmidt & Hunter 1998: meta-analysis of 85 years of selection research found general mental ability was the best single predictor of job performance, with r about .51. Sackett et al. 2022 later argued that statistical corrections inflated some validity estimates, so the exact size is debated.
entries.practice:
1) Stop reading a test score as a ceiling.
2) Name the specific skill behind the score.
3) Practice that skill in a real task.
4) Re-test on the task, not just the test.
entries.myths: Treating IQ as destiny, or as a measure of human worth, turns a useful statistic into a false story.
entries.drill: Pick one skill you avoid and do a 20-minute beginner session daily for 7 days.

entries.title: IQ predicts some outcomes, modestly
entries.science: Higher IQ scores are linked to somewhat better school results, job performance, and health on average. The links are moderate, and they cannot tell you what one person will do. Opportunity, health, personality, and luck also matter.
entries.studies: Schmidt & Hunter 1998: general mental ability predicted job performance at about r = .51 across jobs. Strenze 2007: meta-analysis found IQ predicted later education, occupation, and income.
entries.practice:
1) Use IQ-type tests as one signal, not a verdict.
2) Add a work sample or real task.
3) Track outcomes over months.
4) Judge decisions by results.
entries.myths: Myth: a high IQ guarantees success, or a low IQ rules it out. Correlations describe groups, not individuals.
entries.drill: List three outcomes you care about and one skill plus one habit that affects each; practice the weakest link daily for 7 days.

entries.title: IQ is not destiny, and not morality
entries.science: A test score is a snapshot of performance under particular conditions, not a measure of character or human worth. Scores can change with education, health, sleep, and practice. Honesty, kindness, and judgment are separate from IQ.
entries.studies: Ritchie & Tucker-Drob 2018: meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies found about 1 to 5 IQ points gained per extra year of education. Flynn 1987: IQ scores rose substantially across decades, showing that average performance is not fixed.
entries.practice:
1) Describe people by behavior, not by score.
2) Treat your own score as information.
3) Target a skill you can practice.
4) Reassess after real practice.
entries.myths: Myth: IQ tells you who is good, honest, or kind. It does not measure morality at all.
entries.drill: Write down one label you use about your own ability; replace it for 7 days with a specific skill and a daily practice step.

entries.title: The CHC model, plainly
entries.science: Modern intelligence research often uses the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model, which sorts many narrow skills under broader abilities, and those under g. Two broad abilities matter in daily life: fluid reasoning for new problems and crystallized knowledge for learned facts and words. The model is a map, not a claim that every box is a separate brain module.
entries.studies: McGrew 2009: review described CHC theory as the most widely used framework in modern intelligence testing, organizing narrow, broad, and general abilities.
entries.practice:
1) For a task, label the fluid part and the crystallized part.
2) Train the missing part.
3) Use real problems, not just quizzes.
4) Review what transfers.
entries.myths: Myth: one IQ number captures every mental ability. A full assessment samples several broad abilities.
entries.drill: Choose one skill; list one fluid and one knowledge component, then practice each for 10 minutes daily for 7 days.

entries.title: Tests measure test-taking too
entries.science: A score reflects ability plus familiarity with tests, motivation, anxiety, sleep, language, and culture. The same person can score differently on different days or formats. A test is a sample of behavior, not a direct readout of the brain.
entries.studies: Steele & Aronson 1995: framing a test as diagnostic of ability lowered Black students' performance; later replications of that effect were mixed.
entries.practice:
1) Practice under the real format.
2) Protect sleep the night before.
3) Write down anxious thoughts before the test.
4) Compare scores across conditions, not once.
entries.myths: Myth: a low score proves low potential. It may reflect the conditions of the test.
entries.drill: Before your next test or evaluation, log sleep, anxiety, and preparation for 7 days, then compare with the result.
entries.resource: Intelligence and How to Get It (Nisbett)

entries.title: Takeaway: build skills, not labels
entries.science: Labels feel like explanations, but they do not change behavior. Specific skills, feedback, and practice do. Treat intelligence as a mix of trainable abilities and knowledge, not a fixed identity.
entries.studies: Sisk et al. 2018: two meta-analyses found growth-mindset beliefs and interventions had weak average effects, so mindset slogans alone are not a lever. Ericsson et al. 1993: focused practice with feedback separated higher and lower performers in violinists.
entries.practice:
1) Replace 'I am bad at X' with 'I have not practiced X this way'.
2) Define one sub-skill.
3) Get feedback weekly.
4) Track reps, not moods.
entries.myths: Myth: a fixed label is a fact. It is a prediction that can be tested and often revised.
entries.drill: Replace one 'I am bad at X' statement with 20 minutes of daily practice on a specific X sub-skill for 7 days.

entries.title: Linguistic: useful skill, not a separate intelligence
entries.science: Gardner calls language one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in vocabulary, storytelling, and writing, and those skills can improve. The unsupported part is the claim that verbal skill is an independent intelligence with its own brain system.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: linguistic tests loaded strongly on general intelligence. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validating evidence that the eight intelligences are independent.
entries.practice:
1) Use stories to study a topic.
2) Explain a concept aloud in plain words.
3) Write a one-paragraph summary from memory.
4) Get feedback on clarity.
entries.myths: Myth: strong verbal skill is a separate intelligence that does not overlap with reasoning or knowledge.
entries.drill: For 7 days, explain one idea aloud for 5 minutes and write a three-sentence summary without notes.

entries.title: Logical-mathematical: real aptitude, overlapping with g
entries.science: Gardner calls logic and math one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in numerical and reasoning skill, and practice improves it. The unsupported part is the claim that it is an independent intelligence; reasoning tests load heavily on g.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: arithmetic reasoning tests loaded strongly on g, which contradicts the independence claim. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validating data for MI theory.
entries.practice:
1) Turn a claim into numbers.
2) Estimate before calculating.
3) Solve one word problem daily.
4) Check the answer against the estimate.
entries.myths: Myth: being good with numbers is a separate intelligence unrelated to language and knowledge.
entries.drill: Do one estimation problem and one word problem daily for 7 days, then compare estimates with answers.

entries.title: Spatial: a talent that still shares variance
entries.science: Gardner calls spatial skill one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in mental rotation, map reading, and visual design. The unsupported part is the claim that spatial skill is an independent intelligence; spatial tests also load on g.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: both spatial tests showed substantial g loadings. Waterhouse 2006: review found no evidence that the intelligences operate as separate systems.
entries.practice:
1) Sketch ideas before writing.
2) Use a map or diagram for one task daily.
3) Rotate objects in your mind.
4) Compare your sketch with the source.
entries.myths: Myth: visual talent is a separate intelligence that does not transfer to reasoning.
entries.drill: For 7 days, turn one idea a day into a diagram and redraw it from memory.

entries.title: Musical: a specific talent, not a general intelligence
entries.science: Gardner calls musical ability one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in pitch, rhythm, and musical memory, and those skills can be trained. The unsupported part is calling it an independent intelligence; music tests are often unreliable and overlap with other abilities.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: the music tests had poor reliability and weak g loadings, so the domain was not well measured. Waterhouse 2006: review found no support for eight independent intelligences.
entries.practice:
1) Clap a rhythm before practicing a passage.
2) Learn one short phrase by ear.
3) Use rhythm to chunk information.
4) Record and compare weekly.
entries.myths: Myth: musical skill proves a separate, general intelligence. It is a specific talent, not a brain-wide upgrade.
entries.drill: Practice one short rhythm or melody by ear for 10 minutes daily for 7 days and record it on day one and day seven.

entries.title: Bodily-kinesthetic: motor skill, not a mind module
entries.science: Gardner calls bodily-kinesthetic skill one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in coordination, movement, and craft, and practice improves them. The unsupported part is treating motor talent as a general intelligence; it is better described as a specific skill.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: bodily-kinesthetic tests had low g loadings, suggesting a separate motor talent rather than a general intelligence. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validation for MI theory.
entries.practice:
1) Learn a physical skill in small parts.
2) Practice the hardest part slowly.
3) Film yourself and compare.
4) Add speed only after accuracy.
entries.myths: Myth: being good with your hands means you have a separate intelligence that predicts thinking skill.
entries.drill: Pick one physical skill and practice its hardest sub-movement for 10 minutes daily for 7 days, filming day one and day seven.

entries.title: Interpersonal: social skill is real and trainable
entries.science: Gardner calls understanding others one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in reading social cues and managing relationships, and these skills can improve. The unsupported part is calling social skill an independent intelligence; social tests correlate with general cognition and personality.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: interpersonal tests correlated with g and with other domains. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validating evidence for separate intelligences.
entries.practice:
1) Ask one open question.
2) Summarize what you heard.
3) Check your guess about their feeling.
4) Adjust and follow up.
entries.myths: Myth: social skill is a separate intelligence unrelated to reasoning or knowledge.
entries.drill: Once a day for 7 days, ask one open question, summarize the answer, and check whether your read was right.

entries.title: Intrapersonal: reflection helps, the label does not
entries.science: Gardner calls self-understanding one of eight separate intelligences. The useful part is real: people differ in noticing their own feelings, motives, and limits, and reflection can improve this. The unsupported part is calling it an independent intelligence; self-report measures are weak and often overlap with personality.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: the two intrapersonal measures were uncorrelated, so the domain was not coherent. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validating evidence for MI theory.
entries.practice:
1) Name one feeling and its trigger.
2) Write what you wanted to do.
3) Write what you did.
4) Note the gap without judging.
entries.myths: Myth: self-knowledge is a separate intelligence that guarantees good decisions. Insight helps, but behavior still needs practice.
entries.drill: Keep a three-line evening log for 7 days: feeling, trigger, and one choice you would repeat or change.

entries.title: Naturalist: pattern spotting, thin evidence
entries.science: Gardner added naturalist skill as an eighth intelligence. The useful part is real: people differ in noticing patterns in plants, animals, and materials, and this can be trained. The unsupported part is treating it as a separate intelligence; the evidence for it as a coherent domain is especially thin.
entries.studies: Visser et al. 2006: naturalistic tests shared little variance beyond g, so the domain was not coherent. Waterhouse 2006: review found no validation for the eight-intelligences model.
entries.practice:
1) Observe one natural system closely.
2) Record categories and changes.
3) Make a prediction.
4) Check it the next day.
entries.myths: Myth: a 'naturalist intelligence' is a separate brain system. Pattern spotting in nature is a useful skill, not a separate mind.
entries.drill: For 7 days, spend 10 minutes observing one plant, animal, or outdoor patch and log one pattern and one prediction.

entries.title: Far transfer is the hard part
entries.science: Brain games make you better at the game and at similar tasks. They generally do not make you broadly smarter or improve everyday thinking. The gap between trained tasks and distant outcomes is where most claims fail.
entries.studies: Simons et al. 2016: review of brain-training studies found extensive near transfer, less transfer to closely related tasks, and little evidence of far transfer or everyday improvement.
entries.practice:
1) Name the real task you want to improve.
2) Practice that task directly.
3) Measure the real outcome.
4) Ignore game scores unless they match it.
entries.myths: Myth: 15 minutes of brain games raises IQ. The evidence for broad gains is weak.
entries.drill: Pick one real-world task and practice it directly for 15 minutes daily for 7 days; log only real-task improvement.

entries.title: Working-memory training: real but narrow
entries.science: Working-memory training makes you better at the trained task and similar ones. It does not reliably raise general intelligence or everyday functioning. Near gains are real; far gains are not.
entries.studies: Melby-Lervåg & Hulme 2013: meta-analysis found short-term near transfer from working-memory training but no robust far transfer to intelligence. Melby-Lervåg, Redick & Hulme 2016: review found no convincing evidence of long-term cognitive gains.
entries.practice:
1) Train the task you actually need.
2) Use chunking and notes.
3) Reduce memory load where possible.
4) Re-test the real task.
entries.myths: Myth: a popular working-memory game raises IQ. It mostly improves that game.
entries.drill: Choose a real task that strains memory and practice it 10 minutes daily for 7 days while tracking errors.

entries.title: What actually raises ability: education
entries.science: Schooling is the most consistent lever researchers have found for raising intelligence scores. Each extra year of education is linked to about 1 to 5 IQ points. The gains appear across abilities and can last.
entries.studies: Ritchie & Tucker-Drob 2018: meta-analysis of 142 effect sizes from over 600,000 people found about 1 to 5 IQ points per additional year of education.
entries.practice:
1) Take the hardest course you can handle.
2) Stay in structured learning.
3) Use retrieval and spacing.
4) Finish what you start.
entries.myths: Myth: intelligence is fixed after school. Education effects persist and can appear across the lifespan.
entries.drill: Enroll in or finish one structured course this week and schedule two 45-minute study blocks before day seven.

entries.title: The compounding skill stack
entries.science: Skills combine. A useful stack, such as writing plus statistics plus a domain, is rarer and more valuable than one isolated talent. Small advantages in several skills can compound through better work and opportunities.
entries.studies: Ackerman 1996: theory and evidence showed that abilities, interests, and personality jointly shape how domain knowledge grows over time. Schmidt & Hunter 1998: prior learning and general ability predicted how quickly people learn new jobs.
entries.practice:
1) Pick one core skill.
2) Add one complement.
3) Use both on a real project.
4) Drop a third skill for now.
entries.myths: Myth: only raw talent matters. A well-chosen stack can beat a narrow strength.
entries.drill: List your three strongest skills and use them together on one small project this week.

entries.title: Motivation beats magic
entries.science: No pill, game, or supplement reliably makes you smarter. Motivation helps mainly by increasing practice, and simple mindset slogans do little on their own. The boring levers are the reliable ones: sleep, practice, feedback, and good teaching.
entries.studies: Sisk et al. 2018: meta-analysis found growth-mindset interventions had a small average effect (d about 0.08), so motivation is not magic. Duckworth & Seligman 2005: self-discipline predicted academic performance more strongly than IQ in adolescents.
entries.practice:
1) Make the first step tiny.
2) Put materials in sight.
3) Schedule a fixed slot.
4) Track sessions, not intentions.
entries.myths: Myth: a supplement or app will do the work for you. There is no reliable shortcut.
entries.drill: Schedule a fixed 20-minute study slot for 7 days and put the materials in plain sight the night before each session.

entries.title: Method of loci, step by step
entries.science: The method of loci stores items as vivid images along a familiar route. It borrows the brain's strong spatial memory for lists and speeches. With practice, ordinary people can improve list recall dramatically.
entries.studies: Dresler et al. 2017: six weeks of method-of-loci training raised novices from about 26 to 62 of 72 words recalled, close to memory athletes at about 71, and gains lasted four months.
entries.practice:
1) Choose a familiar route with 10 stops.
2) Place one vivid image at each stop.
3) Walk the route in your mind to recall.
4) Reuse the route, then build a second one.
entries.myths: Myth: memory tricks only work for special people. Novices improved sharply in a controlled training study.
entries.drill: Build one 10-stop route and memorize a 10-item list on it daily for 7 days.

entries.title: Chunking
entries.science: Short-term memory holds only a few chunks at once. Grouping items into meaningful units lets you carry more without adding slots. Expertise often works by building larger chunks.
entries.studies: Cowan 2001: review estimated working-memory capacity at about four chunks. Chase & Simon 1973: chess experts recalled meaningful board positions far better than random positions.
entries.practice:
1) Group numbers into 3-4 digit units.
2) Turn a list into categories.
3) Make a memorable acronym.
4) Recall the groups before the details.
entries.myths: Myth: willpower can expand working memory without limit. Capacity is limited; chunking works around it.
entries.drill: Chunk one phone number, one shopping list, and one password into meaningful groups, then test recall daily for 7 days.

entries.title: Dual coding
entries.science: Words and images create two connected memory traces. Relevant pictures plus words often beat words alone. The pictures must explain the idea, not just decorate it.
entries.studies: Mayer 2009: review of multimedia learning found that relevant words and pictures improved learning more than words alone. Paivio 1986: dual-coding theory proposed separate verbal and imagery systems.
entries.practice:
1) Write the key idea in one sentence.
2) Draw a simple diagram of it.
3) Explain the diagram aloud.
4) Rebuild it from memory.
entries.myths: Myth: more pictures always help. Decorative images can distract and reduce learning.
entries.drill: For 7 days, turn each key idea you study into a rough diagram plus one sentence, then redraw it from memory.

entries.title: Elaborative interrogation
entries.science: Asking why and how connects a new fact to what you already know. The extra processing makes the fact easier to find later. It works best when you answer from memory before checking.
entries.studies: Pressley et al. 1987: answering why-questions improved fact learning compared with reading alone. Dunlosky et al. 2013: review rated elaborative interrogation as moderately useful.
entries.practice:
1) Read one fact.
2) Ask why it is true.
3) Answer from memory.
4) Check and correct.
entries.myths: Myth: re-reading is enough. It feels smooth but often leaves weak memory.
entries.drill: Write five why-questions about one topic and answer each from memory daily for 7 days.

entries.title: Spaced repetition schedule
entries.science: Reviewing at increasing gaps beats cramming for long-term memory. The best gap depends on how long you need to remember. A simple 1-3-7-21 day schedule is enough to start.
entries.studies: Cepeda et al. 2006: meta-analysis of 184 articles (317 experiments, 839 assessments) found spaced practice beat massed practice for verbal recall.
entries.practice:
1) Enter the item on day 1.
2) Review on day 3.
3) Review on day 7.
4) Review on day 21.
entries.myths: Myth: cramming is just as good if the test is soon. It usually fades faster.
entries.drill: Put one item you are learning on a 1-3-7-21 day review schedule and follow it for 7 days.
entries.resource: Remember: The Science of Memory and the Art of Forgetting (Genova)

entries.title: Sleep consolidates memory
entries.science: Sleep after learning helps stabilize and organize new memories. Cutting sleep hurts attention, encoding, and recall. A short review before bed can pair with that consolidation.
entries.studies: Rasch & Born 2013: review found sleep after learning supports memory consolidation. Walker & Stickgold 2006: review linked sleep to offline memory processing.
entries.practice:
1) Keep a fixed bedtime.
2) Aim for 7-9 hours.
3) Review key material 10 minutes before bed.
4) Avoid all-nighters before tests.
entries.myths: Myth: sleep is wasted study time. It is part of learning, not a break from it.
entries.drill: For 7 days, keep a fixed bedtime that gives you 7-9 hours and review key material for 10 minutes before bed.

entries.title: Names and faces routine
entries.science: Names are arbitrary labels, while faces are rich visual patterns. Turn the name into an image and attach it to a distinctive facial feature. Repeating the name and testing yourself seals it.
entries.studies: Yesavage, Rose & Bower 1983: older adults taught interactive imagery and pleasantness judgments recalled more names than controls.
entries.practice:
1) Repeat the name aloud.
2) Pick a distinctive feature.
3) Turn the name into a vivid image.
4) Link image and feature, then test later.
entries.myths: Myth: forgetting names means your memory is failing. Names are arbitrary and need a strategy.
entries.drill: Learn five new names each day with the image-feature method for 7 days, then recall them at day's end.

entries.title: Retrieval practice
entries.science: Pulling information from memory strengthens it more than re-reading. Testing is a learning tool, not just a measurement. The effort is what makes it work.
entries.studies: Roediger & Karpicke 2006: students who tested themselves recalled more a week later than students who re-read the material.
entries.practice:
1) Close the book.
2) Write everything you remember.
3) Check the gaps.
4) Repeat the missed items.
entries.myths: Myth: re-reading is the best way to study. It feels easy but produces weaker long-term recall.
entries.drill: Each study day this week, spend 10 minutes writing everything you remember before checking your notes.

entries.title: Spacing
entries.science: Spreading practice over days beats one long session. Spacing feels harder and slower, but it produces more durable memory. The effect is one of the most reliable in learning research.
entries.studies: Cepeda et al. 2006: meta-analysis of 184 articles (317 experiments, 839 assessments) found spaced practice beat massed practice for verbal recall. Kornell 2009: learners often choose cramming even when spacing works better.
entries.practice:
1) Split study into short sessions.
2) Put sessions on a calendar.
3) Leave gaps between them.
4) Test at the start of each session.
entries.myths: Myth: massed practice is better because it feels fluent. Fluency is a poor guide to retention.
entries.drill: Split one hour of study into four 15-minute sessions across four days this week.

entries.title: Interleaving
entries.science: Mixing different problem types forces you to choose a strategy, which improves discrimination and transfer. Blocked practice feels smoother but often works worse. Interleaving is especially useful when types are easy to confuse.
entries.studies: Rohrer & Taylor 2007: interleaved math practice improved test performance compared with blocked practice. Kornell & Bjork 2008: interleaving improved learning of painting styles even though learners preferred blocking.
entries.practice:
1) Collect problems from three topics.
2) Shuffle them.
3) Solve without labels telling you the type.
4) Review errors by type.
entries.myths: Myth: blocked practice is always best. It can inflate practice performance while hurting transfer.
entries.drill: Make a mixed problem set from three topics you know and do 15 minutes daily for 7 days.

entries.title: Desirable difficulty
entries.science: Conditions that make practice feel harder often improve long-term learning. Spacing, testing, and varied practice are examples. Smooth practice can be a sign that little is being stored.
entries.studies: Bjork & Bjork 2011: review found that spacing, testing, and variation improved retention even when practice performance looked worse.
entries.practice:
1) Choose the slightly harder review method.
2) Delay feedback a little.
3) Vary the setting or format.
4) Judge by a later test.
entries.myths: Myth: if practice feels easy, you are learning. Fluency during practice is not the same as durable learning.
entries.drill: For 7 days, replace one easy review habit with a harder recall task and compare your results on day seven.

entries.title: Generation effect
entries.science: Producing an answer yourself, even a wrong one, beats reading it. Generation creates a stronger memory trace, especially when feedback follows. Guess first, then check.
entries.studies: Slamecka & Graf 1978: words generated from cues were remembered better than words simply read. Bertsch et al. 2007: meta-analysis found a reliable generation effect across studies.
entries.practice:
1) Cover the answer.
2) Generate it from the cue.
3) Check and correct.
4) Repeat missed items.
entries.myths: Myth: reading the answer is as good as producing it. Production adds a retrieval step.
entries.drill: Cover the answers on one set of notes and generate each one from a cue for 10 minutes daily this week.

entries.title: Feynman technique
entries.science: Explaining a concept simply exposes gaps in understanding. It forces retrieval, organization, and generation. If you cannot explain it plainly, you do not understand it yet.
entries.studies: Chi et al. 1994: students who explained material to themselves learned more than students who did not. Feynman's technique is a practice routine built on this self-explanation evidence, not a controlled protocol of its own.
entries.practice:
1) Pick one concept.
2) Explain it to a beginner without notes.
3) Mark every gap.
4) Simplify and repeat.
entries.myths: Myth: recognizing a term means you understand it. Recognition is weaker than explanation.
entries.drill: Explain one concept aloud for 5 minutes daily without notes for 7 days; note one gap and fix it.

entries.title: Teach-back
entries.science: Teaching others, or preparing to teach, improves your own learning. The gain comes from retrieving and organizing the material, not from being an expert. Short lessons with questions work best.
entries.studies: Fiorella & Mayer 2013: students who explained a lesson to others performed better on a transfer test than students who only studied.
entries.practice:
1) Pick a small idea.
2) Teach it in 3 minutes.
3) Ask two questions.
4) Note what you could not explain.
entries.myths: Myth: teaching is only for experts. Preparing to teach is a learning strategy for beginners.
entries.drill: Teach one small lesson to a friend or camera each day for 5 days and list what you could not explain.

entries.title: What deliberate practice is
entries.science: Deliberate practice is focused work on a specific weakness with feedback. It is not just repetition; it is designed to improve a defined part of performance. It is effortful and often not enjoyable.
entries.studies: Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer 1993: study of violinists found top performers had accumulated more deliberate practice hours than less accomplished players.
entries.practice:
1) Define one weakness.
2) Set a success test.
3) Get feedback during practice.
4) Repeat with small adjustments.
entries.myths: Myth: all practice counts. Mindless repetition can plateau for years.
entries.drill: Choose one sub-skill, record a baseline, and do 20 focused minutes daily with feedback for 7 days.

entries.title: What the meta shows
entries.science: Deliberate practice matters, but it explains only part of why people differ. The share is larger in predictable activities like games and music, and smaller in education and professions. Other factors matter too.
entries.studies: Macnamara et al. 2014 (2018 corrigendum): meta-analysis found deliberate practice explained 24% of performance variance in games, 23% in music, 20% in sports, 5% in education, and 1% in professions.
entries.practice:
1) Keep practicing deliberately.
2) Track results, not just hours.
3) Look for other limiting factors.
4) Change the plan if results stall.
entries.myths: Myth: 10,000 hours guarantees expertise. Practice is important but not sufficient.
entries.drill: Estimate your practice hours in one skill, compare them with your results this week, and name one non-practice factor.

entries.title: How to practice deliberately anyway
entries.science: Even a partial factor is worth using if you control it. Target weaknesses, get immediate feedback, and work at the edge of your ability. Short, focused sessions beat long, vague ones.
entries.studies: Ericsson 2008: review of deliberate practice principles emphasized representative tasks, feedback, and repetition. Macnamara et al. 2014: practice explained a meaningful but partial share of performance.
entries.practice:
1) Pick a weakness.
2) Define what good looks like.
3) Get feedback within minutes.
4) Adjust one variable.
entries.myths: Myth: more hours always mean better performance. Without feedback, hours can entrench errors.
entries.drill: Record a 5-minute performance, get one specific critique from a better person, and practice only that point daily for 7 days.

entries.title: The role of coaching
entries.science: A skilled coach can shorten trial and error by spotting errors you cannot see. Feedback raises performance on average, but poor feedback can make it worse. Coach quality matters.
entries.studies: Kluger & DeNisi 1996: meta-analysis found feedback improved performance on average, but about one-third of feedback interventions reduced performance.
entries.practice:
1) Choose a coach with proven results.
2) Ask for one specific correction.
3) Apply it immediately.
4) Test whether it helps.
entries.myths: Myth: any coach is better than none. Bad feedback can cost time and confidence.
entries.drill: Ask one skilled person for one specific critique of your work and apply it for 7 days.

entries.title: Quality vs hours
entries.science: How you practice matters more than the raw hours. Focused, feedback-rich sessions beat distracted ones. But quality cannot erase differences in opportunity, starting age, and biology.
entries.studies: Hambrick et al. 2014: deliberate practice predicted chess performance but explained only about one-third of the variance. Macnamara et al. 2014 (2018 corrigendum): overall, practice explained about 14% of performance variance across domains.
entries.practice:
1) Shorten the session.
2) Remove distractions.
3) Set one goal.
4) Review the recording.
entries.myths: Myth: hours logged equals progress. A log records time, not learning.
entries.drill: Do three 25-minute focused sessions this week and log one improvement from each; compare with your usual practice.

entries.title: Attention is trainable-ish
entries.science: Attention can improve with practice, but gains are usually narrow and modest. Mindfulness training shows small effects on attention. It is not a permanent brain upgrade.
entries.studies: Tang, Hölzel & Posner 2015: review found mindfulness training can improve attention, with small to moderate effects and weak study designs in many trials.
entries.practice:
1) Sit for 10 minutes.
2) Focus on the breath.
3) Notice when the mind wanders.
4) Return without judgment.
entries.myths: Myth: meditation makes you permanently focused. Benefits depend on continued practice and are modest.
entries.drill: Do 10 minutes of focused breathing daily for 7 days and count how often your mind wanders.

entries.title: Multitasking cost
entries.science: The brain switches tasks rather than doing two at once. Switching costs time and increases errors, especially with complex work. Heavy media multitasking is linked to worse attention.
entries.studies: Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans 2001: task switching produced measurable time costs. Ophir, Nass & Wagner 2009: heavy media multitaskers performed worse on tasks that required ignoring distractions.
entries.practice:
1) Do one task at a time.
2) Close other tabs and apps.
3) Batch messages.
4) Note every switch.
entries.myths: Myth: multitasking saves time. It usually adds switching costs.
entries.drill: For 7 days, do one task at a time in 25-minute blocks and log each switch.

entries.title: Phone friction: remove, not resist
entries.science: The mere presence of your phone can drain attention, even when it is face down or off. Willpower is a weak strategy compared with removing the cue. Put the phone out of reach.
entries.studies: Ward et al. 2017: the mere presence of one's smartphone reduced available cognitive capacity in a series of experiments.
entries.practice:
1) Put the phone in another room.
2) Turn off nonessential notifications.
3) Use a blocker during work.
4) Keep a paper list for urges.
entries.myths: Myth: you can just ignore it. The cue can tax attention without your awareness.
entries.drill: Put your phone in another room during work for 7 days and track focus each afternoon.

entries.title: Pomodoro mechanics
entries.science: Short work blocks with breaks make starting easier and reduce fatigue. The 25/5 ratio is a convention, not a law. Choose a block length that fits the task.
entries.studies: Ariga & Lleras 2011: brief diversions improved sustained attention compared with no breaks. Direct evidence for the specific pomodoro ratio is thin, so treat it as a practical default.
entries.practice:
1) Choose one task.
2) Set 25 minutes.
3) Take a 5-minute break.
4) Repeat four times.
entries.myths: Myth: pomodoro is a proven optimal method. It is a useful structure, not a law of attention.
entries.drill: Run four pomodoro cycles daily for 7 days and record when focus drops.

entries.title: Deep-work blocks and attention restoration
entries.science: Long, uninterrupted blocks allow deeper work. Rest and time in nature can restore directed attention. Protect the block before adding more tasks.
entries.studies: Berman, Jonides & Kaplan 2008: walking in nature improved attention performance compared with walking in an urban environment.
entries.practice:
1) Book 60-90 minutes.
2) Remove notifications.
3) Work on one output.
4) Take a short outdoor break.
entries.myths: Myth: constant busyness equals productivity. Fragmented work often produces less.
entries.drill: Book one 90-minute phone-free deep-work block daily for 7 days and take a short outdoor break after.

entries.title: Confirmation bias
entries.science: People seek and favor information that supports what they already believe. This feels like being reasonable, not biased. The fix is to actively look for disconfirming evidence.
entries.studies: Nickerson 1998: review documented confirmation bias across many judgment and memory studies.
entries.practice:
1) State your belief.
2) Write the strongest opposing case.
3) Name what would change your mind.
4) Look for that evidence.
entries.myths: Myth: smart people are immune. Intelligence can make motivated reasoning more elaborate.
entries.drill: For 7 days, write the best case against one belief you hold and one piece of evidence that would change your mind.

entries.title: Base rates
entries.science: Base rates are how common something is in the first place. Ignoring them makes vivid cases feel more likely than they are. A positive test means little when the condition is rare.
entries.studies: Kahneman & Tversky 1973: experiments showed people underused base rates when making predictions.
entries.practice:
1) Ask how common this is.
2) Use counts out of 100.
3) Combine the base rate with the specific evidence.
4) Check the math.
entries.myths: Myth: a vivid case beats a statistic. The case is one data point; the base rate summarizes many.
entries.drill: Find one news claim this week and estimate its base rate before judging the claim.

entries.title: Anchoring
entries.science: Anchoring is when a first number pulls your estimate toward it, even if the number is arbitrary. Anchors show up in prices, negotiations, and sentencing. Make your estimate before hearing theirs.
entries.studies: Tversky & Kahneman 1974: a random starting number shifted participants' estimates, demonstrating anchoring.
entries.practice:
1) Write your estimate first.
2) Build a range.
3) Get an independent estimate.
4) Compare and adjust.
entries.myths: Myth: you are not influenced by irrelevant numbers. Anchoring works even when people know about it.
entries.drill: Before your next purchase or estimate, write your number first, then check the seller's anchor.

entries.title: Availability
entries.science: The availability heuristic is judging frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid news and recent events distort risk perception. Ease of recall is not evidence of likelihood.
entries.studies: Tversky & Kahneman 1973: judged frequency followed ease of recall in experiments on the availability heuristic.
entries.practice:
1) Notice what example comes to mind.
2) Ask what you are not seeing.
3) Find the annual rate.
4) Compare with your gut.
entries.myths: Myth: if you can think of it, it must be common. Memory is not a frequency counter.
entries.drill: Pick one fear this week and find the actual annual rate; compare it with your gut estimate.

entries.title: Loss aversion
entries.science: Losses feel worse than equal gains feel good, often about twice as strong. This makes people avoid sensible risks and cling to bad options. Reframing the choice can loosen the effect.
entries.studies: Kahneman & Tversky 1979: prospect theory showed losses loomed larger than gains in decisions under risk.
entries.practice:
1) Write the loss and the gain.
2) Write the cost of doing nothing.
3) Compare over a year.
4) Choose deliberately.
entries.myths: Myth: loss aversion always protects you. It can keep you in a losing situation.
entries.drill: List one decision you are avoiding; write the cost of inaction for 7 days and compare it with the possible loss.

entries.title: Steelmanning
entries.science: Steelmanning means stating the strongest version of the other side before you respond. It reduces strawman arguments and exposes weaknesses in your own view. It is a skill, not agreement.
entries.studies: Fernbach et al. 2013: asking people to explain an opposing policy in detail reduced the extremity of their attitudes.
entries.practice:
1) State their view fairly.
2) Give their best evidence.
3) Name what you agree with.
4) Then respond.
entries.myths: Myth: steelmanning means giving up your view. It tests your view; it does not require surrender.
entries.drill: Steelman one opposing view each day for 5 days in three sentences, then write your response.

entries.title: Spotting bad studies and misinformation
entries.science: Small samples, no control group, and flexible analyses make findings unreliable. Learning common tricks helps you resist misleading claims. Read the sample size and comparison group before the headline.
entries.studies: Button et al. 2013: review found small sample sizes reduce statistical power and inflate effect sizes in neuroscience. Lewandowsky et al. 2012: review found corrections and prebunking can reduce misinformation influence.
entries.practice:
1) Find the sample size.
2) Check for a control group.
3) Check whether the study was registered in advance or replicated.
4) Read the original source.
entries.myths: Myth: a published study proves a fact. Publication is a step, not a guarantee.
entries.drill: Take one headline claim this week and check its sample size, control group, and original source.

entries.title: Psychology
entries.science: 1) Behavior is shaped by situations as well as personality. 2) Self-reports are shaky, so watch what people do. 3) Many findings are small, so check replications.
entries.studies: Nisbett & Wilson 1977: people confidently gave reasons for behavior that did not match the actual causes. Open Science Collaboration 2015: a large replication project found many psychology effects were weaker than first reported.
entries.practice:
1) Look for a situational cause.
2) Prefer observed behavior to stated motives.
3) Check whether a finding replicated.
4) Test one idea on yourself.
entries.myths: Myth: psychology is just common sense. Experiments often show common sense is wrong.
entries.drill: Watch the first two lectures of Yale's Introduction to Psychology with Paul Bloom on Open Yale Courses this week.
entries.resource: Psychology: A Very Short Introduction (Butler & McManus)

entries.title: Behavioral economics
entries.science: 1) People use mental shortcuts that create predictable errors. 2) Context and defaults strongly shape choices. 3) Incentives matter, but not always in the simple way we expect.
entries.studies: Kahneman & Tversky 1979: prospect theory showed losses loom larger than gains. Johnson & Goldstein 2003: organ donation rates differed sharply depending on the default option.
entries.practice:
1) Notice the default.
2) Precommit before temptation.
3) Reframe losses as gains.
4) Check the incentive actually in play.
entries.myths: Myth: people are rational calculators. Small context changes reliably shift choices.
entries.drill: Work through the first week of MIT OpenCourseWare 14.13 Psychology and Economics with Frank Schilbach this week.

entries.title: Sociology
entries.science: 1) Individual outcomes are shaped by groups, institutions, and networks. 2) Norms and roles guide behavior. 3) Background and structure often explain outcomes that look personal.
entries.studies: Granovetter 1973: weak social ties were more useful for finding jobs than close ties. Durkheim 1897: suicide rates varied with social integration, arguing that social forces shape individual acts.
entries.practice:
1) Map your network.
2) Look for an institutional cause.
3) Join a group that supports your goal.
4) Ask who benefits from a norm.
entries.myths: Myth: outcomes are purely personal. Structure and networks set the odds.
entries.drill: Watch the first three episodes of Crash Course Sociology on YouTube this week.

entries.title: Anthropology
entries.science: 1) Your way of life is one option among many. 2) Cultural practices make sense in their context. 3) Describe before you judge unfamiliar behavior.
entries.studies: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan 2010: samples drawn mostly from Western, educated, rich countries are unusual, so many psychology findings may not generalize. Malinowski 1922: fieldwork argued that apparently strange customs served real social functions.
entries.practice:
1) Describe the practice without judging.
2) Ask what problem it solves.
3) Compare two cultures.
4) Check your own defaults.
entries.myths: Myth: 'human nature' means your culture's habits. Many habits are learned, not universal.
entries.drill: Work through the first week of MIT OpenCourseWare 21A.00 Introduction to Anthropology with Graham Jones this week.
entries.resource: Social and Cultural Anthropology: A Very Short Introduction (Monaghan & Just)

entries.title: Neuroscience basics
entries.science: 1) The brain learns by changing connections. 2) Sleep, exercise, and stress strongly affect thinking. 3) Brain scans are not mind readers, and left-brain/right-brain claims are mostly wrong.
entries.studies: Maguire et al. 2000: London taxi drivers had larger posterior hippocampi, linked to navigation experience, but the design was correlational. Draganski et al. 2004: juggling practice changed gray matter temporarily.
entries.practice:
1) Protect sleep.
2) Move daily.
3) Manage stress before study.
4) Be skeptical of neuromarketing.
entries.myths: Myth: people are left-brained or right-brained. Complex tasks use distributed networks.
entries.drill: Work through the first week of MIT OpenCourseWare 9.01 Neuroscience and Behavior with Gerald Schneider this week.
entries.resource: The Brain: The Story of You (Eagleman)

entries.title: Statistics
entries.science: 1) Sample size and variation determine how much a result can tell you. 2) Correlation is not causation. 3) Base rates and effect sizes matter more than vivid stories.
entries.studies: Ioannidis 2005: analysis argued that many published research findings are false or inflated, especially with small samples and flexible analyses. Open Science Collaboration 2015: replication rates varied widely across psychology studies.
entries.practice:
1) Ask how many people were studied.
2) Ask how big the effect is.
3) Ask what the comparison group was.
4) Check whether the result replicated.
entries.myths: Myth: a small p-value proves a result is true. It only measures how surprising the data would be if there were no effect.
entries.drill: Complete the first unit of Khan Academy Statistics and Probability this week.

entries.title: Game theory
entries.science: 1) Your best move depends on what others do. 2) Repeated interactions can turn selfish games into cooperation. 3) Credible commitments and clear rules change outcomes.
entries.studies: Axelrod 1984: repeated prisoner's dilemma tournaments found that tit-for-tat, a strategy that cooperates first and then copies, performed well. Nash 1950: defined the equilibrium where no player gains by changing strategy alone.
entries.practice:
1) Map the players and payoffs.
2) Ask whether the game repeats.
3) Make your commitment credible.
4) Look for a better stable outcome.
entries.myths: Myth: game theory means being ruthless. Cooperation is often the winning strategy in repeated games.
entries.drill: Watch the first two lectures of Yale's Game Theory with Ben Polak on Open Yale Courses this week.

entries.title: Linguistics and framing
entries.science: 1) Language shapes what is easy to notice. 2) Framing changes judgments without changing the facts. 3) Precise words reduce confusion.
entries.studies: Tversky & Kahneman 1981: framing a medical outcome as survival versus death changed choices. Boroditsky 2001: language habits were linked to different judgments about time.
entries.practice:
1) Restate a claim in neutral words.
2) Ask what frame is being used.
3) Define key terms.
4) Check whether the frame changes the conclusion.
entries.myths: Myth: words are neutral. Word choice changes attention and judgment.
entries.drill: Watch the first three episodes of Crash Course Linguistics on YouTube this week.

entries.title: Philosophy and logic
entries.science: 1) Clarify definitions before arguing. 2) Valid reasoning can still start from false premises. 3) Steelman the other side to test your own view.
entries.studies: Wason 1968: the Wason selection task showed most people fail a simple logic test, revealing limits in everyday reasoning. Johnson-Laird 1983: mental-model theory explained how people reason with possibilities.
entries.practice:
1) Define the terms.
2) List the premises.
3) Look for a counterexample.
4) Check whether the conclusion follows.
entries.myths: Myth: philosophy is just opinion. Logic and argument analysis have testable standards.
entries.drill: Watch the first three episodes of Crash Course Philosophy on YouTube this week.
entries.resource: Think: A Compelling Introduction to Philosophy (Blackburn)

entries.title: AI literacy
entries.science: 1) AI systems find patterns in data and predict, but they do not understand like people. 2) Outputs can be wrong or biased, so verify them. 3) The quality of your question and data shapes the result.
entries.studies: Bender et al. 2021: analysis argued that large language models can reproduce biases and harmful text from training data. Ji et al. 2023: survey documented how large language models can produce fluent false statements.
entries.practice:
1) Verify factual claims.
2) Give context and constraints.
3) Protect private data.
4) Compare outputs from two tools.
entries.myths: Myth: AI is neutral or always right. It reflects data, design choices, and limits.
entries.drill: Complete the first module of AI for Everyone with Andrew Ng on Coursera (free to audit) this week.
entries.resource: Artificial Intelligence: A Very Short Introduction (Boden)

entries.title: The 20-hour sprint
entries.science: You can reach a useful beginner level in a skill in about 20 hours of focused practice. The method works by breaking the skill down and removing friction. It does not make you an expert.
entries.studies: Kaufman 2013: described the 20-hour method and reported his own practice experiments; it is a heuristic, not a controlled trial. Ericsson et al. 1993: expert performance was associated with years of deliberate practice.
entries.practice:
1) Define the outcome.
2) Break the skill into parts.
3) Remove barriers.
4) Practice 45 minutes daily.
entries.myths: Myth: 20 hours makes you an expert. It gets you to a useful beginner level.
entries.drill: Choose one skill and do a 20-minute beginner session daily for 7 days; list what to practice next.

entries.title: Pick a field: interest plus leverage
entries.science: Pick a field where interest and leverage overlap. Interest keeps you practicing; leverage means the skill helps your work or life. The overlap is where self-study survives.
entries.studies: Ackerman 1996: abilities, interests, and personality jointly shaped the growth of domain knowledge over time. Deci & Ryan 2000: self-determination theory argued that intrinsic motivation supports persistence and deeper engagement.
entries.practice:
1) List three interests.
2) List three leverage points.
3) Circle the overlap.
4) Test it for a week.
entries.myths: Myth: pick the highest-paying field and ignore fit. Low interest makes sustained study hard.
entries.drill: List three fields; for each, write one real use and one week of test material, then start the best fit.

entries.title: A study plan that survives
entries.science: Plans fail when they depend on motivation and have no fixed cue. Small scheduled sessions with a clear next action survive. An if-then plan helps you restart after interruptions.
entries.studies: Gollwitzer 1999: meta-analysis found implementation intentions, or if-then plans, improved goal attainment across many studies.
entries.practice:
1) Choose a fixed time and place.
2) Write an if-then plan.
3) Define the smallest session.
4) Track completion.
entries.myths: Myth: a detailed six-month plan beats a daily habit. Long plans often collapse without a cue.
entries.drill: Write one if-then plan for a daily 20-minute study slot and follow it for 7 days.

entries.title: Test yourself for real: explain it
entries.science: If you can explain a topic clearly to someone else, you probably understand it. If you cannot, you have found a gap. Explanation is a test you can run alone or with a listener.
entries.studies: Fiorella & Mayer 2013: students who explained a lesson to others performed better on a transfer test than students who studied for themselves. Chi et al. 1994: self-explanation improved understanding.
entries.practice:
1) Explain without notes.
2) Answer two questions.
3) Note gaps.
4) Revisit and explain again.
entries.myths: Myth: recognition equals understanding. Being able to pick an answer is not the same as explaining it.
entries.drill: Explain one thing you learned to a person or camera each day for 7 days and write down one gap.

description: History and art as conversation capital: one good story beats ten facts.

entries.title: One good story beats ten facts
entries.science: People remember stories and attach them to you. A recited fact feels like a quiz; a story with a person, a problem, and a turn feels like a gift.
entries.know: Aim to carry a few vivid stories, not an encyclopedia. For each one, know the setup, the twist, and why you care.
entries.story: The Bayeux Tapestry tells the Norman conquest of England in dozens of scenes, like a medieval comic strip. It is propaganda, which is exactly why it works as a story.
entries.words: "I would rather hear one story you love than ten facts you memorized."

entries.title: Breadth plus fascination, not trivia hoarding
entries.science: Interesting people connect fields. They use one area to light up another, which is why a little history can make a science story land.
entries.know: Learn a thin layer across many fields, then go deeper in two or three you love. Depth gives you authority; breadth gives you bridges.
entries.story: The Antikythera mechanism, found in a Greek shipwreck in 1901, is a bronze gear device from around 100 BCE that modeled the heavens. Ancient people built a mechanical cosmos before they had a word for computer.
entries.words: "I love that someone built a model of the sky out of bronze gears. It makes the ancient world feel less distant."

entries.title: Culture is conversation capital
entries.science: Shared references let strangers relax. A film, a building, or a song gives you a safe common ground before you get personal.
entries.know: Keep a short list of works you can talk about honestly: one book, one film, one album, one building, one painting.
entries.story: When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, people did not just celebrate with speeches. They climbed the wall and painted it, turning a barrier into a canvas.
entries.words: "I think the test of a good cultural reference is whether it opens a conversation or closes one."

entries.title: Snobbery kills charm
entries.science: Taste is a door, not a wall. People shut down when culture is used to rank them, and open up when it is used to include them.
entries.know: Share what you love without grading the other person. Say 'this hit me' rather than 'you should know this.'
entries.story: Marcel Duchamp put a urinal in an art show in 1917 and called it 'Fountain.' The point was not that it was beautiful; the point was to ask who gets to decide what art is.
entries.words: "I can love something and still laugh at how seriously I take it."

entries.title: Farming made cities possible
entries.science: For most of human history we moved with food. Farming let people store surplus, and stored surplus let some people build, write, and rule.
entries.know: Farming appeared independently in several places, including the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, and West Africa. Surplus, not farming alone, is what built cities.
entries.story: Around 10,000 BCE, people in the Fertile Crescent began planting wheat and barley. By about 3200 BCE, scribes in Mesopotamia were pressing wedge marks into clay to track grain and beer.
entries.words: "Cities are basically a side effect of storing food. Writing came next, to count it."
entries.resource: Crash Course World History: The Agricultural Revolution

entries.title: River valleys built the first big states
entries.science: Rivers gave water, transport, and fertile mud. That combination supported dense populations and the bureaucracy needed to manage them.
entries.know: Mesopotamia grew between the Tigris and Euphrates; Egypt along the Nile; the Indus cities such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro along the Indus; early China along the Yellow River.
entries.story: The Indus cities had streets laid out on a grid and drains under the roads, around 4,500 years ago. Their writing remains undeciphered, so we still cannot read their names for things.
entries.words: "We have the plumbing but not the language. That is a strange kind of silence."

entries.title: Greece tried democracy; Rome built law
entries.science: Most modern political arguments are reruns. Knowing the original experiments makes the current version easier to see.
entries.know: Athens developed direct democracy around 508 BCE, though only adult male citizens could vote. Rome developed republic and legal forms, including the Twelve Tables around 450 BCE.
entries.story: Athenian citizens could vote to exile a prominent politician for ten years by scratching his name on a pottery shard. The practice was called ostracism, and it is where the English word comes from.
entries.words: "The Greeks invented the vote and the smear campaign at roughly the same time."
entries.resource: Crash Course World History: Ancient Greece

entries.title: World religions in one line each
entries.science: Religion shapes art, law, food, and daily manners. A respectful one-line map keeps you from confusing traditions or treating them as one single thing.
entries.know: Judaism: ancient covenant tradition centered on the Torah. Hinduism: a family of traditions with the Vedas, dharma, karma, and moksha. Buddhism: Siddhartha Gautama's teaching on suffering and the Eightfold Path. Christianity: Jesus of Nazareth and the Bible, emerging in the 1st century CE. Islam: Muhammad and the Quran, emerging in the 7th century CE, with the Five Pillars. Sikhism: Guru Nanak's teaching in 15th-century Punjab, with the Guru Granth Sahib as scripture.
entries.story: The Golden Rule appears in many traditions in different words, from Confucius to Hillel to Jesus. The shared shape is striking, even when the beliefs behind it are not.
entries.words: "I like learning the one-line version first, then letting someone correct it. It is a door, not a verdict."

entries.title: The Silk Road moved more than silk
entries.science: Trade routes are idea routes. Goods travel with stories, technologies, and microbes, which is why the medieval world was more connected than it looks.
entries.know: Overland and Indian Ocean routes linked China, India, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. Paper, printing, gunpowder, religions, and the plague all moved along them.
entries.story: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 and killed perhaps a third of its people. It traveled along the same trade routes that carried silk and spices.
entries.words: "The Silk Road was less a road than a relay race, and everyone was passing more than goods."
entries.resource: The Rest Is History: Silk Road episodes

entries.title: Renaissance and the printing press
entries.science: The Renaissance revived old texts, and printing made those texts cheap enough to spread. Together they changed who could learn and argue.
entries.know: The Renaissance began in Italian cities in the 14th century and spread north. Gutenberg's press in the 1440s combined movable metal type with a screw press; within decades, presses operated across Europe.
entries.story: Gutenberg's first big project was a Bible, printed around 1455. Early printers copied the look of handwritten manuscripts, because that was the look buyers trusted.
entries.words: "Printing did to knowledge what the internet is doing again, five centuries later."
entries.resource: Crash Course World History: The Renaissance

entries.title: The Enlightenment turned ideas into revolutions
entries.science: Arguments about rights, consent, and reason moved from salons to barricades. The results shaped the modern state and its contradictions.
entries.know: Locke argued for natural rights; Rousseau for the general will; Voltaire attacked religious intolerance. The American Revolution (1776), French Revolution (1789), and Haitian Revolution (1791) put these ideas under pressure.
entries.story: The Haitian Revolution turned the richest colony in the Caribbean into the first modern state born from a successful slave revolt. It is often left out of the Enlightenment story, even though it tested its claims hardest.
entries.words: "The Enlightenment is a promise and a scorecard. The interesting part is the gap."
entries.resource: Crash Course World History: The French Revolution

entries.title: Industry remade time and work
entries.science: The industrial revolution changed where people lived, how long they worked, and what childhood meant. Its effects are still in your commute and your clock.
entries.know: It began in Britain in the late 18th century with steam power, textiles, and iron, then spread. Factories pulled people to cities and created new social classes.
entries.story: Early factory workers often worked 12-hour days or longer, and children were used to reach under machines. Reformers fought for limits, which is why the weekend and the eight-hour day exist at all.
entries.words: "The weekend is not ancient. It is a hard-won invention."
entries.resource: Crash Course European History: The Industrial Revolution

entries.title: The 20th century compressed everything
entries.science: Two world wars, decolonization, the Cold War, and the internet happened within a few lifetimes. That speed is why older relatives can feel like time travelers.
entries.know: Key markers: World War I (1914), World War II (1939-45), Indian independence and partition (1947), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989), the web (1989-91), and the smartphone (2007).
entries.story: ARPANET sent its first message in 1969: 'LO.' The system crashed before the full word 'LOGIN' could be sent, so the first internet message was a partial failure.
entries.words: "The internet's first word was a crash. That feels weirdly on brand."

entries.title: Maurya and Gupta: empire and golden age
