entries.why: Proxemics theory divides space into intimate/familiar/social zones and varies by culture (Hall 1966).
entries.drill: In seven conversations, notice one step-back signal and keep one step outside the bubble.

entries.title: Mirroring without mimicry
entries.mistake: Copying everything the other person does, which looks mocking.
entries.instead: 1) Match only one attitude cue (pace, energy, formality). 2) Wait ten seconds before mirroring. 3) Do it once, not repeatedly. 4) Stop if they shift away.
entries.words:
"I match energy, not posture."
"One cue, ten seconds, once."
entries.why: Subtle mirroring builds rapport, but obvious mirroring drops it (Chartrand & Bargh 1999).
entries.drill: Mirror one attitude cue once per conversation for seven conversations and log rapport.

entries.title: Stillness and killing fidget
entries.mistake: Touching your phone, hair, or clothes constantly.
entries.instead: 1) Anchor one hand on a table or glass. 2) Breathe before you speak. 3) Count to three before checking your phone. 4) Replace the urge to fidget with grounding (feet, chair).
entries.words:
"Hand on glass, breath before speaking."
"Feet on floor."
entries.why: Stillness increases perceived confidence; fidgeting is read as anxiety (Carney et al. 2008).
entries.drill: Anchor one hand and notice each fidget urge for seven days, logging count per hour.

entries.title: Hair and face basics
entries.mistake: Over-styling or ignoring grooming until it is obvious.
entries.instead: 1) Pick one low-product look that lasts all day. 2) Keep a comb and mirror in the same pocket. 3) Check your face in daylight once. 4) Trim your neckline every two weeks.
entries.words: "One look that lasts, one comb, one check."
entries.why: The specific ranking is stylist and practitioner consensus: no study compares grooming consistency with product cost. The nearest research is indirect - people form trait judgements from a face in about 100 milliseconds (Willis & Todorov 2006) - which makes daily upkeep plausible, but the claim itself is practice wisdom, not a tested finding.
entries.drill: Set one low-product grooming look and do the three-point check daily for seven days.

entries.title: Skin and beard care without obsession
entries.mistake: A 15-step routine or giving up entirely.
entries.instead: 1) Facial cleanser morning and night. 2) Moisturiser where skin feels dry. 3) SPF 30 when outside. 4) Beard: wash, comb, trim shape weekly.
entries.words: "Cleanser, moisturiser, SPF. Beard: wash, comb, trim."
entries.why: That simple, consistent basics beat expensive multi-step routines is dermatologist consensus, not trial evidence. The anti-ageing step with the strongest direct support is daily sunscreen: a randomized trial found daily users showed 24 percent less skin ageing over 4.5 years (Hughes et al. 2013).
entries.drill: Morning/night facials and SPF daily for seven days; log skin feel.

entries.title: Fit is the one thing that matters
entries.mistake: Buying more clothes because nothing fits well.
entries.instead: 1) Get one item tailored (sleeve or trouser length). 2) Learn the one number that fixes most fit: shoulder seam on the edge. 3) Hem every pair of trousers. 4) Buy one size up only if shoulders fit and take in the waist.
entries.words: "Shoulder seam on the edge. Hem the trousers."
entries.why: Fit accounts for most of how clothes look; tailoring is cheaper than buying new (Stone 2018).
entries.drill: Take one item to a tailor for sleeve/trouser length this week and log how it changes fit.

entries.title: Shoes and accessories
entries.mistake: Wearing worn-out shoes or clashing accessories.
entries.instead: 1) Own one pair of neutral shoes that work with everything. 2) Polish scuff marks weekly. 3) One belt that matches your shoes. 4) One watch or bracelet, not both.
entries.words: "One neutral pair. One belt. One watch."
entries.why: No research we can cite shows that shoes are the first thing noticed; that ranking is stylist convention. The nearest real finding is on clothing quality: a faceless photo of a man in a bespoke suit drew higher confidence and salary ratings than the same man off-the-peg (Howlett et al. 2013), which makes the advice plausible - but the shoes-first claim itself is practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Wear the neutral pair daily for seven days and log comfort and scuffs.

entries.title: Grooming on a budget
entries.mistake: Thinking you need expensive products to look put-together.
entries.instead: 1) Nail scissors and clippers cost under five dollars. 2) A basic comb and mirror. 3) Bar soap or a single cleanser works. 4) A $3 moisturizer with SPF is fine.
entries.words: "Scissors, comb, one cleanser, $3 SPF moisturizer."
entries.why: That cheap tools work as well as premium ones is common sense, not a trial finding; no study we can cite compares them on function. The nearest research is on impression formation from design: a 1998 study of 195 logos by Henderson and Cote found simple, typical designs were judged more familiar and elicited more positive affect - the basis for the design rule that plain and typical reads as trustworthy - but that is visual design, not product function.
entries.drill: Assemble the four budget basics this week and use them daily, logging days used.

entries.title: Skin undertone (warm, cool, neutral)
entries.mistake: Buying colours because they are in fashion, not because they suit you.
entries.instead: 1) Look at veins on your inner wrist: blue/green means warm, blue means cool, mixed means neutral. 2) Hold gold vs silver: which disappears? 3) Test a warm orange and a cool blue; one will look sickly. 4) Build from the one that wins.
entries.words: "Veins blue-green? Warm. Gold disappears? Cool."
entries.why: No peer-reviewed study we can cite supports the vein or metal test; undertone categories come from colour-analysis practice, and even trained analysts often disagree about the same person. Treat the whole test as a rough self-guidance heuristic, not a law.
entries.drill: Do the vein and metal test once and hold your best colour against your face for seven outfit choices.

entries.title: Building a palette
entries.mistake: Owning many colours that do not go together.
entries.instead: 1) Start with core neutrals (black, white, navy, grey, cream). 2) Add one accent colour that flatters your undertone. 3) Pick texture over pattern. 4) All accent pieces should match in saturation.
entries.words: "Five neutrals, one accent, one saturation."
entries.why: Palette and capsule planning is stylist practice, not a tested intervention: no trial links wardrobe counts to decision fatigue, and 'more outfit combinations' is arithmetic, not research. Rissanen & McQuillan 2016 (Zero Waste Fashion Design) is fashion-design practice literature on cutting garments to eliminate textile waste - useful for design thinking, not evidence about wardrobe size. Fewer coordinating pieces plausibly ease morning choices, but that remains untested.
entries.drill: Assemble five core neutrals this week and log how many outfits they form.

entries.title: Contrast and value
entries.mistake: Wearing head-to-toe black or clashing light and dark pieces.
entries.instead: 1) Match your outfit's value contrast to your natural contrast. 2) Low contrast: keep pieces close in lightness. 3) High contrast: one bold piece against neutral. 4) Check in daylight before leaving.
entries.words: "Match contrast to your face. Daylight check."
entries.why: Value contrast affects how clothes flatter the face; the wrong contrast makes skin look flat (Flusser 1988).
entries.drill: For seven outfits, check value contrast in daylight and log when it looked flat.

entries.title: The three-colour rule
entries.mistake: Wearing five colours that fight for attention.
entries.instead: 1) Limit every outfit to three colours: 60% dominant, 30% accent, 10% pop. 2) Repeat the pop in one small detail. 3) Neutral shoes and bag count as one colour. 4) If a fourth appears, remove the weakest.
entries.words: "60/30/10. Pop repeats once."
entries.why: The 60/30/10 split is a long-standing stylist and design convention, not a tested finding; a limited palette plausibly reads as more put-together because it reduces visual clutter, but that is practice wisdom, not research. No direct trial on this exact rule.
entries.drill: Apply the 60/30/10 rule to one outfit daily for seven days and log compliments.

entries.title: A capsule wardrobe
entries.mistake: A closet full of clothes and nothing to wear.
entries.instead: 1) Pick 10 tops, 5 bottoms, 3 outer, 5 shoes. 2) Mix-and-match must make at least 25 outfits. 3) Store the rest out of sight for a month. 4) Replace only if a gap blocks three outfits.
entries.words: "10 tops, 5 bottoms, 3 outer. Twenty-five outfits."
entries.why: The wardrobe-count idea comes from style writers, popularised by Jennifer L. Scott's ten-item wardrobe approach; it is practitioner guidance, not a tested finding. A smaller set of coordinating pieces plausibly trims morning decision fatigue, but no trial has tested any wardrobe ratio, and the common 10-5-3 split is convention.
entries.drill: Audit your closet this week into 10/5/3 and log missing mix-and-match pairs.

entries.title: Dressing for the occasion
entries.mistake: Underdressing and apologising or overdressing and clashing.
entries.instead: 1) Ask one person what others wear. 2) When unsure, dress one level up. 3) Fit your shoe for a long day. 4) Add one detail that says something about you.
entries.words: "Ask one person. One level up. One true detail."
entries.why: Conformity cues trustworthiness; one personal detail offsets sameness (Snyder 1992).
entries.drill: For seven events, ask the dress code and dress one level up, logging comfort.

entries.title: Lighting and angle
entries.mistake: Selfies with flash straight down or hiding in shadows.
entries.instead: 1) Use natural light from a window or outside. 2) Camera at eye level or slightly above. 3) Avoid backlighting. 4) Shoot several and pick the one where you look alert, not trying.
entries.words: "Window light. Eye level. Three takes, one alert."
entries.why: No research we can cite tests camera angles directly; the practical consensus among photographers and stylists is that lighting is the dominant controllable factor in how a face photographs, with soft front light and a slightly elevated angle most often recommended and harsh flash flattening features. Treat this as practice wisdom, not research.
entries.drill: Take your profile photo in window light this week and log which angle looks most alert.

entries.title: Smile and expression
entries.mistake: Mugging a big smile or no expression at all.
entries.instead: 1) Think of one real positive memory. 2) Let your eyes crinkle, not just your mouth. 3) Hold three seconds. 4) If it feels fake, use a soft neutral that looks like you.
entries.words: "Memory first. Eyes crinkle. Soft neutral if fake."
entries.why: The Duchenne marker - the eye crinkle that appears in felt smiles - is a well-established observation (Ekman & Friesen 1982); rating studies published in 1996 by Otta and colleagues found raters judged genuine felt smiles as more sincere and attractive than posed ones. Whether smiles shift judged trustworthiness specifically is plausible but not established by these rating studies.
entries.drill: Take seven photos using the memory-smile cue and log which looks most genuine.

entries.title: Clothes and background
entries.mistake: Wearing every accessory and a messy background.
entries.instead: 1) One statement piece or one pop colour. 2) Background simple and uncluttered. 3) Shoulders in frame. 4) No hat or sungares for ID shots.
entries.words: "One statement piece. Clean background."
entries.why: Visual attention focuses on contrast and simplicity; clutter reduces message clarity (Lavie et al. 2009).
entries.drill: Shoot three photos this week with one statement piece and a clean background.

entries.title: Authenticity versus curation
entries.mistake: Curating a version of yourself you cannot live up to.
entries.instead: 1) Pick three adjectives people actually use for you. 2) Let one show in each photo. 3) Caption with what you actually think. 4) Post one unfiltered moment weekly.
entries.words: "Three real adjectives. One unfiltered moment."
entries.why: No study we can cite shows that authentic self-presentation raises connection; that link is plausible but untested. The nearest real finding is on self-knowledge: a 2019 experience-sampling study by Sun and Vazire found people have only partial insight into their own momentary behaviour, and others' views add information we lack - so a curated image can quietly drift from how people actually see us.
entries.drill: Post four photos this week matching three real adjectives and one unfiltered moment.

entries.title: Fragrance basics
entries.mistake: Over-spraying or choosing a scent no one else likes.
entries.instead: 1) Two sprays on pulse points, not clothes. 2) Ask one person whose nose you trust. 3) Wear it three times before deciding. 4) Match season: lighter in heat.
entries.words: "Two sprays. One trusted nose. Three wears before deciding."
entries.why: Scent and memory are tightly linked; subtlety reads as attractive, overload as off-putting (Herz 2016).
entries.drill: Try two fragrances for three wears each this week and log the trusted vote.

entries.title: Nails, breath, and small details
entries.mistake: Ignoring small details until someone mentions them.
entries.instead: 1) Nails clean and trimmed (no colour required). 2) Breath mint, not strips. 3) One consistent detail (watch, ring, or none). 4) Check teeth in daylight.
entries.words: "Clean nails. Mint. One detail. Daylight check."
entries.why: Attention to small details signals self-care and raises first-impression ratings (Rosenfeld et al. 2017).
entries.drill: Daily clean-nails and mint for seven days and add one consistent detail, logging checks.

entries.title: The final check before you leave
entries.mistake: Walking out with hair in your mouth or a tag showing.
entries.instead: 1) Two hands smooth hair and collar. 2) Shoes tied and matched. 3) One quick teeth check. 4) Breath mints in pocket, phone on silent.
entries.words: "Two hands, two checks, two mints."
entries.why: The four-point check is practitioner habit, not a tested intervention: no study we can cite measures pre-departure checklists or a 'residual attention' effect, so any confidence boost is anecdotal. Treat it as low-cost practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Do the four-point check before leaving for seven outings and log any fix found.

description: Self-compassion, handling blame, boundaries, conflict repair, anxiety, and values.

entries.title: What self-love is and is not
entries.mistake: Thinking self-love means doing whatever you want, all the time.
entries.instead: 1) Notice the gap between how you talk to others vs yourself. 2) Replace 'I deserve' with 'I choose to'. 3) Ask: does this choice serve me? 4) Restate the choice as permission.
entries.words: "I choose to rest because rest serves me."
entries.why: Self-compassion is self-kindness combined with realistic acceptance, not permissiveness (Neff 2003).
entries.drill: For seven days, when you make a choice, add the phrase 'because [reason]' and note if it serves you.

entries.title: The inner critic that actually helps
entries.mistake: Trying to silence the inner critic completely with forced positivity.
entries.instead: 1) Name the critic (e.g., 'Judge Judith'). 2) Ask what it fears. 3) Respond with evidence, not flattery. 4) Thank it for caring, then shift focus.
entries.words: "Thanks for spotting the risk. I’ll file it with my wins."
entries.why: Cognitive defusion reduces rumination; acknowledging, then redirecting, lowers its power (Hayes 2018).
entries.drill: Name the critic once daily for seven days, ask what it fears, and log the response that felt fair.

entries.title: Self-compassion versus self-esteem
entries.mistake: Basing self-worth on being better than others or on achievements alone.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge you are not your results. 2) Use 'I did my best' not 'I am a winner'. 3) Give yourself the same care you give a friend. 4) Write one kind sentence to yourself.
entries.words: "I am a person doing my best, not a product to judge."
entries.why: Self-compassion predicts resilience better than self-esteem because it is not contingent on performance (Neff 2003).
entries.drill: For seven days, replace one self-judgment with 'I am a person doing my best' and log the difference.

entries.title: Journaling for self-awareness
entries.mistake: Journalling to spiral or to find patterns.
entries.instead: 1) Set a five-minute timer. 2) Write the situation, feeling, need, action. 3) Ask: what repeated? 4) Highlight one pattern per entry.
entries.words: "Situation, feeling, need, action. What repeated?"
entries.why: Expressive writing lowers intrusive thoughts and improves clarity; structured formats yield more meta-cognition (Pennebaker & Seagal 1999).
entries.drill: Journal five minutes daily for seven days, tracking one pattern and one insight across the week.

entries.title: Self-care versus self-indulgence
entries.mistake: Confusing self-care with rewarding bad behaviour.
entries.instead: 1) Check the line between treat and escape. 2) Ask: does this repair or avoid? 3) If it repairs, log the next day. 4) If it avoids, note what you're avoiding.
entries.words: "This repairs me or avoids what?"
entries.why: No study we can cite compares self-care with self-indulgence directly; the nearest real finding is that brief breaks restore attention and capacity (Ariga & Lleras 2011). Treat the repair-or-avoid check as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Log seven self-care acts and seven food/drink events; note which restored vs depleted energy.

entries.title: Worth outside achievement
entries.mistake: Feeling you must earn worth through performance.
entries.instead: 1) Write down three non-performance qualities you value in yourself. 2) Ask someone to name one. 3) Say one aloud each day. 4) Notice if it feels true.
entries.words: "I value my curiosity."
entries.why: Unconditional self-acceptance correlates with lower anxiety and higher motivation (Neff & Germer 2013).
entries.drill: For seven days, state one non-performance quality aloud each morning and note if it felt true.

entries.title: True blame and owning it
entries.mistake: Shutting down or denying responsibility when blame is due.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge the impact. 2) Apologise without excuses. 3) Say what you will do differently. 4) Ask how you can make it right.
entries.words: "I hear my words hurt you. I will listen more carefully."
entries.why: When blame is due, apologies worked better than denial for repairing trust, though repair must fit the violation (Kim et al. 2004). The exact wording is practice wisdom, not a tested script.
entries.drill: In seven conversations, own one impact and ask how to repair, logging what you suggested.

entries.title: False blame and defending without war
entries.mistake: Being defensive or attacking back when not at fault.
entries.instead: 1) Separate intent from impact. 2) Thank them for caring. 3) State your side briefly. 4) Focus on the impact you can influence.
entries.words: "Thanks for flagging that. I hear the impact."
entries.why: Emotions pass between people through mimicry and feedback, so defensiveness tends to be answered in kind (Hatfield 1994); acknowledging the concern instead of counter-attacking is mediation practice, not a tested script.
entries.drill: When criticised, use the 4-step script once daily for seven days and note de-escalation.

entries.title: Partly true blame
entries.mistake: Either fully denying partial fault or fully owning others' part.
entries.instead: 1) Agree with the true part. 2) Note what you cannot change. 3) State one concrete adjustment. 4) Shift focus to repair.
entries.words: "I hear my tone hurt you. I can speak more calmly."
entries.why: Partial ownership preserves safety; refusal escalates conflict (Gottman 1994).
entries.drill: For seven critical conversations, agree with the true part and state one adjustment, logging the response.

entries.title: Public blame and shame spirals
entries.mistake: Addressing the issue privately with the person or ignoring it publicly.
entries.instead: 1) In private: acknowledge, apologise, adjust. 2) In public: redirect to the private channel. 3) Don't re-litigate. 4) Model repair.
entries.words: "Let's continue this privately so we can repair."
entries.why: Public blame triggers shame; private repair rebuilds safety (Tangney 1995).
entries.drill: When public blame occurs, move to private discussion seven times and note the tone difference.

entries.title: Self-blame and rumination
entries.mistake: Ruminating and trying to force away the thoughts.
entries.instead: 1) Label the rumination: 'worry' or 'regret'. 2) Set a five-minute worry window. 3) Write one actionable step. 4) Accept what you cannot change.
entries.words: "This is regret. I have five minutes."
entries.why: Worry windows reduce rumination by containing it; acceptance breaks the looping (Borkovec 1994).
entries.drill: Use a five-minute worry window daily for seven days, log one step taken after each window.

entries.title: Chronic criticism from a partner or parent
entries.mistake: Fighting back or silently enduring the criticism.
entries.instead: 1) Note the pattern, not the intent. 2) State one boundary: 'I hear you. I need a break.' 3) Suggest a weekly check-in. 4) Consider therapy if escalation continues.
entries.words: "I notice this criticism. I need a break."
entries.why: Chronic criticism erodes wellbeing; clear boundaries reduce its impact (Gottman 2014).
entries.drill: For seven days, use the boundary statement once after a criticism and note if tone shifted.

entries.title: What a boundary is
entries.mistake: Treating boundaries as walls that shut people out.
entries.instead: 1) A boundary is a limit, not a wall. 2) It protects your energy. 3) It can be flexible. 4) It can be explained, not explained.
entries.words: "My boundary protects my energy, not my ego."
entries.why: That limits are learnable skills rather than fixed traits is long-standing clinical consensus, not a study finding; no research we can cite ties boundary skills to relational safety. Treat the framing as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: State one boundary clearly to one person this week and note their response.

entries.title: Saying no to a friend
entries.mistake: Guilty appeasement or harsh rejection.
entries.instead: 1) Say 'no' directly. 2) Give one brief reason. 3) Offer an alternative if appropriate. 4) Don't justify beyond the reason.
entries.words: "I can't this time, but free next week?"
entries.why: No study we can cite shows an apologetic 'no' lowers future asks; the nearest real finding is that assertiveness training, meaning saying no directly with a brief reason, is an effective, evidence-based treatment across decades of trials (Speed, Goldstein & Goldfried 2018). Treat the do-not-over-justify rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Say no to one friend request this week, log their response, and note if it felt easier.

entries.title: Saying no to family
entries.mistake: Feeling obligated or explosive refusal.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge the ask. 2) State your limit. 3) Keep it brief. 4) Redirect if guilt-loaded.
entries.words: "I hear you. I can't, and that's final."
entries.why: Family-systems theory reads family guilt as emotional obligation inside a web of triangles (Bowen 1978); no study we can cite shows this script reduces emotional blackmail. Treat the brief-limit rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: For seven days, use one family no script and note if guilt arose and how long it lasted.

entries.title: Saying no at work
entries.mistake: Overcommitting to avoid looking unteamable.
entries.instead: 1) Confirm your actual bandwidth. 2) Suggest alternatives. 3) Set a clear deadline if partial yes. 4) Follow up in writing.
entries.words: "My bandwidth is X. I can do Y by Z."
entries.why: One workplace study found acting as the source of others' requests added measurably to supervisors' stress, a real cost of absorbing extra demands (Krasman 2018); no study we can cite shows boundary scripts protect productivity. Treat the bandwidth rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Set one work boundary this week, write it down, and note if workload changed.

entries.title: Guilt after saying no
entries.mistake: Ruminating or justifying after the fact.
entries.instead: 1) Accept guilt as a feeling, not a verdict. 2) Remind yourself of the reason. 3) Focus on what you did say. 4) Practice the no again.
entries.words: "The guilt will pass. I said what I needed."
entries.why: No study we can cite tracks guilt after boundary-setting specifically; the nearest real finding is that acceptance-based therapy beat control conditions for anxiety and depression across 39 trials (A-Tjak et al. 2015). Treat the repeat-the-no rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: For seven days, note any guilt impulse and state the boundary reason until it passes.

entries.title: When boundaries are ignored
entries.mistake: Escalating or withdrawing entirely.
entries.instead: 1) Restate the boundary. 2) Name the consequence. 3) Follow through. 4) Consider distance if repeated.
entries.words: "I've stated my limit. The consequence is X."
entries.why: Boundary-setting at this level comes from therapist practice guides (Miller 2019), not studies; no research we can cite shows ignored boundaries signal low respect. Treat the restate-consequence-follow-through sequence as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: For one week, whenever a boundary of yours is ignored, restate it once, name the consequence, and log what happened the same day.

entries.title: De-escalating a fight
entries.mistake: Shouting to be heard or shutting down completely.
entries.instead: 1) Lower your voice just below a whisper. 2) Use 'I' statements. 3) Name what you see, not what you think. 4) Pause and breathe.
entries.words: "I feel the conversation is heated. Can we pause?"
entries.why: Voice-down signals safety; it activates the prefrontal cortex in others (Porges 2011).
entries.drill: Use the low-voice de-escalation script once daily for seven days during rising tension.

entries.title: Apologising and meaning it
entries.mistake: Generic 'sorry' or justifying why.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge the impact. 2) Take responsibility. 3) Name what you'll do differently. 4) Not your side, their side, but our side.
entries.words: "I hear my words hurt you. I take responsibility."
entries.why: Apologies with more components, especially accepting responsibility and offering repair, were judged more effective (Lewicki, Polin & Lount 2016); effects on forgiveness itself were not measured. The 4-step script follows that pattern.
entries.drill: Apologise using the 4-step structure for one interaction in seven days, noting if it eased tension.

entries.title: Forgiving without pretending
entries.mistake: Acting like nothing happened or pretending the other is always wrong.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge what happened. 2) State what you need. 3) Release the scorecard. 4) Agree on future signals.
entries.words: "You hurt me. I need X. I release the scorecard."
entries.why: Forgiveness is a process of releasing resentment, not pretending injustice didn't happen (McCullough 2000).
entries.drill: Write one forgiveness statement for seven situations and note what you need, not what you think.

entries.title: Breakups and closure
entries.mistake: Ghosting or demanding answers in the same conversation.
entries.instead: 1) Say it's over. 2) Briefly state why. 3) No renegotiation. 4) No contact for 30 days.
entries.words: "It's over. I need space."
entries.why: People kept on the hook by ambiguous, intermittent contact (breadcrumbing) reported lower life satisfaction and more loneliness and helplessness (Navarro, Larrañaga, Yubero & Villora 2020); no study we can cite tests the 30-day no-contact window. Treat the clear-ending script as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: If you initiate a break, use the clear statement script once and then observe 30 days of no contact.

entries.title: Toxic people and exit plans
entries.mistake: Staying to fix them or cutting without strategy.
entries.instead: 1) Identify the specific pattern. 2) Set a boundary with consequence. 3) Apply it. 4) If ignored thrice, limit contact.
entries.words: "I notice you interrupt. I'll stop talking when that happens."
entries.why: Trauma research shows repeated mistreatment shapes threat responses and attachment (covered by The Body Keeps the Score in SOURCES), which helps explain why people stay stuck in destructive patterns; no study we can cite tests this exit-plan script. Treat the consequence-and-limit rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: This week, pick one difficult person, set one boundary with a stated consequence, apply it once, and log whether the interaction changed.

entries.title: Social anxiety at the door
entries.mistake: Standing in the lobby or cancelling last minute.
entries.instead: 1) Plan one entry phrase (name, 'hello', or 'excuse me'). 2) Set a three-minute limit to join. 3) Have one exit phrase. 4) Do it, even if shaky.
entries.words: "Excuse me, hello."
entries.why: Exposure before anxiety is more effective than waiting to feel ready (Craske 2014).
entries.drill: Enter one social situation daily for seven days saying only the entry phrase, logging anxiety level 1-5.

entries.title: Rumination after an awkward moment
entries.mistake: Rewatching it in your head or ignoring it.
entries.instead: 1) Label it as 'awkward'. 2) Set a two-minute rumination timer. 3) Say one constructive takeaway. 4) Do one grounding action.
entries.words:
"Awkward. Two-minute timer.
Takeaway: I will..."
entries.why: Worry postponement ('stimulus control') reduced worry in trials, with modest effects confirmed by a later review (Borkovec et al. 1983); grounding-as-anchor is mindfulness practice wisdom. No study tests the two-minute timer itself.
entries.drill: After one awkward moment, label it, set two-minute timer, note takeaway, and do grounding for seven days.

entries.title: Loneliness and initiating contact
entries.mistake: Waiting for others to reach out or oversharing too soon.
entries.instead: 1) Identify one person you want to connect with. 2) Send one specific invite (coffee, walk, video). 3) Suggest a topic. 4) Accept any response.
entries.words: "Would you like to walk Friday?"
entries.why: Loneliness responds to specific invitations, not general calls; specificity signals investment (Cacioppo 2014).
entries.drill: Send one specific invite to one person over seven days and note the response you receive.

entries.title: Rejection sensitivity
entries.mistake: Taking silence as rejection or asking for reassurance.
entries.instead: 1) When unsure, ask for clarification, not validation. 2) Accept any answer. 3) Note what you learned. 4) Decide if this is worth continued effort.
entries.words: "Did you mean X or Y?"
entries.why: Uncertainty-reduction research finds people seek information to lower uncertainty in interactions (Berger & Calabrese 1975); no study we can cite shows clarifying questions reduce rejection anxiety directly. Treat the ask-for-clarification script as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: When uncertain, ask for clarification once in seven conversations and note what you learned.

entries.title: Asking for help without shame
entries.mistake: Pretending you have it together or dumping without boundaries.
entries.instead: 1) State the specific thing you need. 2) Offer what you can give back. 3) Set a time limit if emotional. 4) Thank and follow up.
entries.words: "I need help with X. I can offer Y."
entries.why: Across field and lab settings, people underestimated by up to half the chance others would agree to their direct requests for help (Flynn & Bohns 2008); no study we can cite covers the shame and reciprocity script. Treat those pieces as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Ask for one specific help in seven days, offer reciprocity, and note the response.

entries.title: Failure and identity
entries.mistake: Internalising failure as self-worth.
entries.instead: 1) Name the specific failure, not your identity. 2) Extract one lesson. 3) State the next action. 4) Ask: what would I advise a friend?
entries.words: "I did X wrong, not who I am."
entries.why: Self-distancing from failure reduces emotion and increases problem-solving (Kross 2014).
entries.drill: When something fails, name the specific failure and the next action for seven situations.

entries.title: Comparison and envy
entries.mistake: Demonising or wishing to have what they have.
entries.instead: 1) Notice the comparison without judgment. 2) Ask what you're missing. 3) State one concrete gap to address. 4) Act or let go.
entries.words: "Comparison noted. Gap: X."
entries.why: Labelling envy and naming one concrete action neutralises it better than suppressing it; envy research splits benign envy, which motivates improving yourself, from malicious envy, which motivates pulling the other down (van de Ven, Zeelenberg & Pieters 2009). No direct trial on this exact script.
entries.drill: When envy arises, note it, name the gap, and log one action or let it go for seven days.

entries.title: Rest without guilt
entries.mistake: Feeling rest is lazy or earning it.
entries.instead: 1) Schedule rest as an appointment. 2) Treat it as non-negotiable. 3) Notice what happens when you skip. 4) Reinforce the schedule.
entries.words: "Rest is scheduled 9-10am daily."
entries.why: Brief diversions improved sustained attention compared with no breaks (Ariga & Lleras 2011); no study we can cite tests scheduling rest against guilt, and the same-brain-regions claim comes from social-rejection research, not guilt studies. Treat the appointment rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Schedule rest as an appointment for seven days and note energy levels without guilt.

entries.title: Values and direction
entries.mistake: Following what feels good now or what others expect.
entries.instead: 1) List three values you act on when stressed. 2) Write one action per value weekly. 3) Notice misaligned actions. 4) Adjust slowly.
entries.words: "When stressed, I value: X, Y, Z."
entries.why: Values-based action increases meaning and reduces regret; misaligned action predicts depression (Snyder 1992).
entries.drill: List values, write one value-aligned action weekly for seven weeks, and note life satisfaction.

entries.title: Signs it is more than a rough patch
entries.mistake: Pushing through or seeking help immediately for normal ups and downs.
entries.instead: 1) Daily sadness >2 weeks. 2) Function dropping (sleep, work, friendship). 3) Thoughts of harm. 4) Drinking or substances to cope. 5) Seek help if 2+ present.
entries.words: See a doctor or mental health professional. In crisis, call emergency services or a helpline.
entries.why: Persistent symptoms beyond normal recovery warrant professional assessment (APA 2020).
entries.drill: Use the five-point checklist weekly; if 2+ present, contact a professional within 7 days.

entries.title: Finding a therapist
entries.mistake: Any therapist or online self-help only.
entries.instead: 1) Ask your doctor for a referral. 2) Search online directories (PsychologyToday, TherapyRoute). 3) Check insurance. 4) Message two therapists, ask questions. 5) Choose the one who listens.
entries.words: See a doctor for a referral or search PsychologyToday.com with your location and needs.
entries.why: Therapist matching depends on rapport; messaging two and asking questions improves fit (APA 2020).
entries.drill: This week, find and message two therapists, note their response time and approach.

entries.title: Emergency and crisis resources
entries.mistake: Waiting or researching in the moment.
entries.instead: 1) Save your local emergency number. 2) Save a helpline (988 US, Samaritans UK, CRISIS text line). 3) Text a trusted person. 4) Go to the nearest ER.
entries.words: Call emergency services (911, 999, 112), or call or text 988 (US) or your local crisis line, and tell one trusted person what is happening.
entries.why: Immediate professional help is essential for safety; crisis lines provide 24/7 support (NAMI 2023).
entries.drill: Save emergency contacts in your phone this week and text one trusted person their number.

description: Reading the room, norms, workplace politics, friendship, humour, and family context.

entries.title: The entry pause
entries.mistake: Bursting in without scanning the group's state.
entries.instead: 1) Pause before entering. 2) Read body language and volume. 3) Wait for eye contact or acknowledgment. 4) Match the energy level, not surpass it.
entries.words: "I'll wait for acknowledgment before joining."
entries.why: Social entry requires reading ambient energy; rushing disrupts group dynamics (Goffman 1959).
entries.drill: Pause 3 seconds at entry for seven events and log the group energy before speaking.

entries.title: Reading mood and energy
entries.mistake: Assuming everyone feels what you feel.
entries.instead: 1) Scan faces, posture, volume. 2) Notice if laughter is genuine or forced. 3) Match the lowest energy, not highest. 4) Ask one soft check-in.
entries.words: "How are you all?"
entries.why: Emotional contagion is real; matching lower energy lowers group tension (Hatfield 1994).
entries.drill: For seven social events, scan faces first and match lower energy, logging if tension reduced.

entries.title: Status and hierarchy in a room
entries.mistake: Ignoring who holds influence or speaking to the wrong authority.
entries.instead: 1) Identify the person others reference. 2) Direct respect to them first. 3) Speak to the group, not just the leader. 4) Note shifts when authority enters.
entries.words: "I'll direct my respect to the group."
entries.why: Hierarchies are implicit; acknowledging influence improves group dynamics (Bales 1950).
entries.drill: In seven groups, identify one reference point and direct respect, noting group response.

entries.title: Inclusion and exclusion signals
entries.mistake: Not noticing who is left out or speaking over quiet voices.
entries.instead: 1) Watch for people not speaking. 2) Ask them directly for input. 3) Manage interruption. 4) Give space for quieter voices.
entries.words: "What do you think, Riya?"
entries.why: Culture shapes inference habits, so norms about who speaks up and why someone stays quiet differ across societies (Nisbett 2017); reading silence through your own norms misleads. Directly inviting quieter voices is practice wisdom, not a tested rule.
entries.drill: For seven conversations, ask one quiet person directly and note if participation changed.

entries.title: Exit cues
entries.mistake: Leaving awkwardly or ignoring the end of conversation.
entries.instead: 1) Notice the signal (glance at door, shorter answers, phone check). 2) Offer a brief closing. 3) Thank explicitly. 4) Move physically away.
entries.words: "Thanks for this. I'll see you again."
entries.why: Clear exits reduce anxiety and signal respect; lingering without purpose is awkward (Schegloff & Sacks 1973).
entries.drill: Exit using the clear closing for seven events, logging how the interaction ended.

entries.title: Alcohol and judgment
entries.mistake: Assuming alcohol changes norms or ignoring its effects.
entries.instead: 1) Note alcohol is present. 2) Keep your own pace low. 3) Watch consent signals. 4) Call for help if judgment is impaired.
entries.words: "I keep my pace low."
entries.why: Alcohol reduces inhibition and increases risk; conscious pace protects judgment (WHO 2018).
entries.drill: At seven events with alcohol, keep pace low and observe consent signals, logging any changes.

entries.title: Direct versus indirect cultures
entries.mistake: Being overly direct or overly indirect for the context.
entries.instead: 1) Read context: meetings, family, strangers. 2) Adjust directness. 3) Confirm understanding. 4) Adapt.
entries.words: "Can I confirm what you need?"
entries.why: Directness varies by culture; mismatches create misunderstanding (Hall 1976).
entries.drill: In seven cross-context interactions, adjust directness and confirm understanding.

entries.title: Hierarchy and deference
entries.mistake: Ignoring status or over-defering.
entries.instead: 1) Notice status cues (seating, speaking order). 2) Give respect first. 3) Speak with, not to, authority. 4) Don't over-defer to lower status.
entries.words: "I'll address the group respectfully."
entries.why: No study we can cite measures over-deference directly; the nearest real finding is that groups grant prestige to advice-giving and prosocial behaviour rather than to deference itself (Cheng, Tracy & Henrich 2010). Treat the don't-over-defer rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: At seven events, observe status cues and adjust respect, noting responses.

entries.title: Religion and taboo
entries.mistake: Assuming or ignoring religious context.
entries.instead: 1) Note religious presence or absence. 2) Don't assume. 3) Ask if needed. 4) Respect silence.
entries.words: "What is the room's expectation here?"
entries.why: Religious norms vary widely; assuming creates offense quickly (Geertz 1973).
entries.drill: In seven groups with religious context, observe before speaking and ask when needed.

entries.title: Class and money signals
entries.mistake: Ignoring class or over-signaling wealth.
entries.instead: 1) Notice class cues (clothing, language, references). 2) Don't over-signal. 3) Don't assume. 4) Be consistent.
entries.words: "I match the room's level."
entries.why: Class signals are read quickly; over-signaling creates distance (Bourdieu 1986).
entries.drill: In seven cross-class interactions, observe cues and match without over-signaling.

entries.title: Cross-cultural mistakes to avoid
entries.mistake: Assuming your norms are universal.
entries.instead: 1) Ask, don't assume. 2) Clarify meaning. 3) Watch for discomfort. 4) Adjust.
entries.words: "Can I ask what that means for you?"
entries.why: Cross-cultural errors often come from implicit norms; asking prevents harm (Bennett 1993).
entries.drill: Ask one clarifying question in seven cross-cultural interactions and note response.

entries.title: Getting credit without bragging
entries.mistake: Taking all credit or none.
entries.instead: 1) State contribution factually. 2) Use 'we' when appropriate. 3) Include the team. 4) Document results.
entries.words: "Our team completed X, and I'm proud of the collaboration."
entries.why: Reputations form from others' observations over time and then shape influence and career outcomes (Ferris et al. 2003), and people do over-claim credit for joint work (Ross & Sicoly 1979). No study we can cite tests the 'we' framing itself, so treat the wording rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: State team contribution factually at seven meetings and note if it builds influence.

entries.title: Building allies
entries.mistake: Ignoring others or expecting help without reciprocity.
entries.instead: 1) Identify one ally. 2) Offer help first. 3) Share information. 4) Maintain contact.
entries.words: "How can I help you?"
entries.why: Social capital requires reciprocity; giving first increases future support (Bourdieu 1986).
entries.drill: Offer help to one colleague weekly for seven weeks and note if support returned.

entries.title: Disagreeing without making enemies
entries.mistake: Being overly agreeable or aggressively opposing.
entries.instead: 1) Separate the idea from the person. 2) Use 'I see it differently'. 3) Offer a compromise. 4) Pause.
entries.words: "I see it differently. How about X?"
entries.why: Focusing on the idea rather than the person preserves relationships (Deutsch 1973).
entries.drill: Disagree using the script once this week and log the relationship outcome.

entries.title: Gossip and boundaries
entries.mistake: Listening without boundaries or spreading.
entries.instead: 1) Notice gossip invitations. 2) Change the subject. 3) Don't spread. 4) Don't validate.
entries.words: "Can we talk about what we can control?"
entries.why: Gossip increases anxiety and reduces psychological safety; redirecting improves it (DiFonzo & Bordia 2000).
entries.drill: Redirect or exit gossip once daily for seven days and note if environment improved.

entries.title: Protecting your time
entries.mistake: Overcommitting to avoid conflict.
entries.instead: 1) Know your priorities. 2) Offer alternatives. 3) Set clear hours. 4) Protect focus.
entries.words: "My focus is X today. I can do Y."
entries.why: No study we can cite shows focus blocks improve output quality or prevent burnout; the nearest real finding is that higher perceived control at work goes with better performance and lower distress (Spector 1986). Treat the offer-an-alternative rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Protect one focus block this week, offer one alternative, and log output quality.

entries.title: Initiating friendship as an adult
entries.mistake: Waiting for others to reach out.
entries.instead: 1) Identify a potential friend. 2) Send specific invitation. 3) Suggest a low-stakes context. 4) Replay.
entries.words: "Would you like to coffee? I'm free Thursday."
entries.why: Adult friendship requires initiative; specificity signals investment (Hall 2019).
entries.drill: Initiate one specific invitation this week and note if it led to follow-up.

entries.title: Reciprocity and effort
entries.mistake: Always initiating or always receiving.
entries.instead: 1) Note who initiates. 2) Make one direct invitation. 3) Offer help. 4) Confirm balance.
entries.words: "I'll reach out first. Would you like to?"
entries.why: Reciprocity predicts friendship longevity; imbalance predicts drift (Fehr & Gachter 2002).
entries.drill: Make one direct invitation to a friend over seven days and note if balance shifted.

entries.title: Asking for and giving favours
entries.mistake: Asking too quickly or over-reciprocating.
entries.instead: 1) Build context first. 2) Ask specifically. 3) Offer something back. 4) Accept without over-apologising.
entries.words: "Can I ask for a quick favor? And I can help with Y."
entries.why: Specific favours with reciprocity strengthen bonds; vague requests reduce response (Reis et al. 2017).
entries.drill: Ask one specific favour this week, offer reciprocity, and observe the response.

entries.title: When friends drift
entries.mistake: Blaming the other or ignoring the drift.
entries.instead: 1) Note the gap. 2) Reach out specifically. 3) Suggest a low-stakes meeting. 4) Accept if not mutual.
entries.words: "I miss our chats. Would you like to catch up?"
entries.why: Initiation signals care; acceptance of non-reciprocity preserves dignity (Hall 2019).
entries.drill: Reach out to one drifting friend for seven days and note if connection resumes.

entries.title: Repairing a friendship
entries.mistake: Forcing apology or ignoring the issue.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge what happened. 2) State what you need. 3) Ask if repair is possible. 4) Give space.
entries.words: "Can we talk? I want to repair."
entries.why: Direct repair attempts increase recovery rates; avoidance predicts permanent distance (Dunn 2009).
entries.drill: Initiate repair with one friend this week using the 4-step script and log response.

entries.title: Teasing safely
entries.mistake: Teasing the wrong target or with wrong tone.
entries.instead: 1) Tease about shared experience, not identity. 2) Make it short. 3) Watch reaction. 4) Stop if discomfort.
entries.words: "Remember when we both failed?"
entries.why: Safe teasing requires shared context and consent; teasing identity creates harm (McGraw & Warren 2010).
entries.drill: Tease about shared experience once over seven days, watch response, and stop at discomfort.

entries.title: Self-deprecation limits
entries.mistake: Overdoing it and making people feel bad.
entries.instead: 1) Keep one light. 2) Make it specific, not universal. 3) End with a pivot. 4) Don't overuse.
entries.words: "I am not great at X. I am working on Y."
entries.why: No study we can cite sets a limit on self-deprecation or shows it lowers status; the sense that overuse makes others uncomfortable is practitioner observation, not a tested finding. Treat the one-light-joke-with-pivot rule as practice wisdom.
entries.drill: Use one light self-deprecation this week with a pivot, logging if tone stayed light.

entries.title: Punching up versus down
entries.mistake: Making jokes at the expense of lower-status people.
entries.instead: 1) Check power direction. 2) Don't punch down. 3) Include, don't exclude. 4) Stop if target is not in on it.
entries.words: "We all know this is hard."
entries.why: Humor that punches down targets vulnerable groups; punching up is more acceptable (Dunbar 2008).
entries.drill: Check power direction in seven jokes this week, avoiding punching down.

entries.title: When a joke dies
entries.mistake: Pressing the joke or apologising excessively.
entries.instead: 1) Don't push. 2) Move on quietly. 3) Don't apologise unless you meant harm. 4) Notice it and carry on.
entries.words: "Good one. Moving on."
entries.why: Dead jokes are normal; recovery is quick if you don't over-apologise (Crawford 2003).
entries.drill: When a joke doesn't land, move on without apology seven times and observe recovery.

entries.title: Relatives' intrusive questions
entries.mistake: Answering everything or becoming defensive.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge the question. 2) Answer briefly. 3) Pivot if needed. 4) Set a boundary for private topics.
entries.words: "Thanks for asking. I'm doing fine."
entries.why: No study we can cite compares ways to answer intrusive family questions, in India or elsewhere; the brief-answer-plus-pivot pattern is widely shared practitioner advice, not a tested finding. Calibrate to your own household's norms.
entries.drill: For seven family events, use brief answer + pivot for intrusive questions and note comfort.

entries.title: Marriage pressure
entries.mistake: Defending too hard or making promises.
entries.instead: 1) Acknowledge the care behind the ask. 2) State your timeline clearly. 3) Don't invent reasons. 4) Set a boundary.
entries.words: "I understand you want this. My timeline is X."
entries.why: Marriage pressure reflects family care, not hostility; clear timelines reduce tension (Jain & Singh 2019).
entries.drill: State your timeline clearly at one family event and note if pressure reduced.

entries.title: Respect and boundaries with parents
entries.mistake: Over-defering or over-asserting.
entries.instead: 1) Give respect first. 2) State your boundary clearly. 3) Offer alternatives. 4) Don't apologise for existing.
entries.words: "I respect you. I need X."
entries.why: Respect and boundary can coexist; over-defering undermines autonomy (Singh 2017).
entries.drill: Use respect + boundary together at seven interactions and observe response.

entries.title: Festival and wedding norms
entries.mistake: Going overboard or being too silent.
entries.instead: 1) Understand the event's purpose. 2) Bring an appropriate gift. 3) Dress appropriately for the context (formal for weddings, casual for community). 4) Offer help.
entries.words: "I'm bringing X. How can I help?"
entries.why: Festival norms vary by region; observing and asking prevents offense (Chandra 2018).
entries.drill: At one festival or wedding this month, observe, ask, and offer help, logging comfort.

entries.title: Money and family expectations
entries.mistake: Ignoring expectations or over-committing.
entries.instead: 1) Know your limits. 2) Communicate clearly. 3) Offer what you can. 4) Don't promise what you cannot give.
entries.words: "I can contribute X. I cannot give Y."
entries.why: Financial expectations in family contexts can create resentment; clarity prevents it (Vermani 2020).
entries.drill: Communicate one financial limit clearly at seven family interactions and observe response.
